subjects.introduction: The heart, one of the Hidden Words declares, is God’s own home, to be sanctified for His descent. It is first of all a dwelling to be cleared for a Guest, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá confesses that nothing he could write would convey the intimacy realized in its essence. The Báb calls the inmost heart, the fu’ád, the greatest of God’s gifts, the seat of His Name, the House of His Oneness; whoever enters it knows God as far as a creature can. Bahá’u’lláh calls the balance of the inmost heart the one measure that never strays, and swears that if people opened the eye of the heart they would see the Truth as existing and all else as nothing. Heart and inmost heart are therefore not words for feeling but capacities of recognition. Psalm 51, asking for a clean heart and a renewed spirit, suggests that perceiving may depend on what one becomes [1]. The path leads on into intuition and inspiration, the degrees of faith and certitude, and the Kingdom the purified heart is said to enter.
subjects.arc: Enter through the heart as a home, explore its capacity for recognition, and approach the limits of what inward experience can express.

order.why: Introduce the heart as a measure of understanding.
Open with the heart as a home awaiting its Guest.
Let intimacy precede abstract accounts of spiritual faculties.
shortened: O spiritual friend! Whatever I might say and whatever I might write, I cannot express and explain the reality of the intimacy and fellowship that has been realized in the essence of the heart.

order.why: Connect inward openness with heavenly inspiration.
shortened: When Saint Paul was asked about certain philosophical questions, he answered that before he had news of Christ, he knew everything, but when he received news of Christ, he became unaware of everything. For Christ so infused him that no room remained for anything else. This heart became empty and filled with Christ, meaning divine outpourings and heavenly inspirations.

order.why: Consider purification as preparation for recognition.
Encounter the distinctive language of the inmost heart.
shortened: Know that God, glorified be He, hath made the greatest of His gifts to the people of possibility the faculty of the heart [fu'ad], and the possessors of understanding have agreed, with the confirmation of the All-Merciful, on this purpose, as their master hath spoken and recorded with the pen of ink that the heart is the highest faculty of man. God hath made this faculty the seat of His exalted Name, the repository of His impenetrable mystery, and the station of His knowledge for the people of proclamation.

order.why: Describes the inmost heart of the Temple as a treasury and dawning-place of divine knowledge.
Place this faculty within a sequence of spiritual capacities.
Distinguish an inwardly established recognition from a borrowed one.
shortened: Should these inmost realities be signs that are securely established within the mirrors of their heart, and not the mere transitory and borrowed ones, they would return unto their true habitations, in both the Beginning and the Resurrection.

order.why: Ask what it means to perceive through the heart.
shortened: I swear by the Sun of the horizon of My Cause that were they to open the eye of the heart, all would behold the Truth as existing and all else as non-existent.

order.why: Retain the brief fragment without supplying its missing context.
shortened: In this hour when the hosts of holy fragrances and the waves of attraction are surging from all directions, and the might of the piercing meteor is driving away and casting out all people of vain imaginings, when the lights of the Kingdom are shining forth and the mysteries of the Realm of Power are manifesting and appearing, when the sea of favors is surging and the lamp of the gathering is brightly lit - this servant has made the pen a means to express the degrees of love for the Ancient Beauty, and has made words the interpreter of meanings, that perchance a verse from the scripture of attraction which is folded within the essence of the heart might be inscribed upon page and paper.

order.why: Consider the reported connection between inward condition and healing.
Turn from receiving light toward writing upon the heart.
Explore interpretation as transformation rather than description alone.
shortened: And verily this is the spirit of the elixir of knowledge whereby the servant ascendeth from all that is still unto the station of motion, and manifesteth the causes of his existence in the degree of the effect, and the fruit of the final cause in the degree of the object and its realm.

This is the saying of Rida - peace be upon him - that "the possessors of understanding know not what is there save through what is here." Until this day none hath opened the door of that knowledge whereby the letters are raised unto the station of His detachment and brought unto the mystery of His unity.

order.why: Return to the language of encounter and fellowship. Allow even familiar spiritual aspirations to be questioned. End at the threshold of what language cannot encompass.
shortened: 28 If the mystic knowers be among them that have attained the beauty of the Beloved, this station is the throne of the inmost heart and the secret of divine guidance. This is the seat of the mystery "He doeth what He willeth, and ordaineth what He pleaseth." Should all that are in heaven and on earth attempt to unravel this exalted allusion and subtle mystery, from now until the Day whereon the Trumpet shall sound, yet would they fail to comprehend even a letter thereof, for this is the station of God's immutable decree and His foreordained mystery. Hence, when asked regarding this matter, He made reply: "It is a bottomless sea that none shall ever fathom." And when the question was repeated, He answered: "It is the blackest of nights through which none can find his way."

order.why: Read a scholar’s account alongside the passage it illuminates.
Examine the contrasting hearts described in the Báb’s terminology.
shortened: The heart (qalb) is the foremost place of appearance (mazhar) of the fu'ad and is in reality two hearts. One is the place of the First Intellect (al-'aqlu'l-awwal), which is the heart of Muhammad, and the other is opposite which is the place of Universal Ignorance....

order.why: Consider the limits of intellect and the heart’s middle way.
Relate inward understanding to unity and action.

questions: How do the images of a home, a mirror, and a throne change your understanding of the heart?
What might distinguish purification of perception from simply feeling certain that one is right?
Where do these passages place the limits of intellectual explanation, and what forms of inquiry remain possible there?
How might a deeper inward understanding become visible in the way we treat another person?

neighbors.invitation: Examine how an inward impression might be tested rather than automatically trusted.
Consider why a mirror’s potential to reflect still calls for assistance and preparation.

references.label: 1 · Psalm 51:10–17 — a renewed heart
references.note: The psalm connects renewal of the heart with repentance, restored joy, and a contrite spirit. Compare this prayerful approach with the compilation’s accounts of the heart as a place of knowledge and encounter. What relationship emerges between moral change and the capacity to perceive?

subjects.introduction: The eye takes a mirage for water and the moving earth for something fixed; insight corrects the eye. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá begins with the superiority of inward perception and then asks the harder question: if inspiration is an influx of the heart, and the promptings of temptation are also an influx of the heart, how is one to tell them apart? The subject lives between two convictions. On one side stands Bahá’u’lláh’s promise that the earnest seeker will be given a new eye, a new ear, a new heart and a new mind, and will find in every atom a door to certitude. On the other stands the plain statement that inspiration, like sense, reason and tradition, is not free from error, so that prayer, effort, evidence and humility remain necessary. Paul held both together when he told the Thessalonians not to quench the Spirit and yet to test everything and keep what is good [1]. Receptivity that does not surrender judgment is a discipline worth learning, and it leads on to the inmost heart, to the mystical vision, and to the spiritual foundations on which true knowledge rests.
subjects.arc: Begin with a perceptual mistake, question inward certainty, and move toward a receptive understanding that remains willing to test itself.

order.why: Start with the arresting contrast between mirage and insight.
shortened: Know thou, verily, insight (i.e., mental perception) sees that which sight (i.e., physical) seeth not, and apprehends that which the eye perceives not. Inasmuch as the sight sees the mirage as water, and the images pictured in a mirror as reality and genuine; and it sees the earth as stationary, and the great stars as small. But the insight corrects the mistake of the Sight, and apprehends the reality; and it sees that the mirage is not water, that the images pictured in mirrors are naught else save reflections, that the earth is moving and the distant stars are great.

order.why: Bring the possibility of error into the inward realm.
shortened: The fourth criterion I have named is inspiration through which it is claimed the reality of knowledge is attainable. What is inspiration? It is the influx of the human heart. But what are satanic promptings which afflict mankind? They are the influx of the heart also. How shall we differentiate between them? The question arises: How shall we know whether we are following inspiration from God or satanic promptings of the human soul?

order.why: Keep the question of competing promptings before the reader.
shortened: The inspiration of God is a revelation to the heart: but temptations of the devil are also addressed to the heart. If to the hearts of men is revealed a command,- " Do ye thus and thus,"- how are we to know whether this is a revelation from God, or a temptation from Satan?

order.why: Explore insight supported by spiritual teachings.
Distinguish initial acceptance from inward assurance.
Open the possibility of renewed spiritual senses. Close with the promise of newly awakened faculties.
shortened: Then will the manifold favors and outpouring grace of the holy and everlasting Spirit confer such new life upon the seeker that he will find himself endowed with a new eye, a new ear, a new heart, and a new mind. He will contemplate the manifest signs of the universe, and will penetrate the hidden mysteries of the soul. Gazing with the eye of God, he will perceive within every atom a door that leadeth him to the stations of absolute certitude. He will discover in all things the mysteries of divine Revelation and the evidences of an everlasting manifestation.

order.why: Give receptivity a musical image.
shortened: But, I swear by God, none heareth and no soul perceiveth, for this divine flute needeth a plectrum of the essence of spirit, and this eternal harp requireth the melody of light - not these remote souls who have never tasted the wine of nearness nor drunk the water of reunion from the matchless fountain.

order.why: Consider the reported appreciation of Quaker inward searching.
Read personal counsel within its reported setting.
Encounter a reported medical anecdote without turning it into advice.
Make the fallibility of inspiration explicit.
Distinguishes divine inspiration from ordinary impressions and identifies divine grace as its source and criterion.
Return to the difficulty of weighing inward voices.
Confront the danger of following mere imaginings.
shortened: We forbade the people from following delusion that they might recognize the manifest Sovereign and that which proceedeth from Him.

order.why: Explore a sequence of different kinds of light.
shortened: To illustrate: There are four kinds of lights: 1 - The outward (or phenomenal) light, which makes things manifest or visible, but which does not discover them. 2 - The light of the eye, or the Eye-sight. This makes things manifest and also discovers them, but it does not comprehend them. 3 - The light of the Intellect (or reason). this light makes things manifest, discovers them, comprehends them, but things pre-exist it, (i.e., its existence is posterior to the creation of things). 4 - The Light of God. It is the revealer of things (i.e., by it things are made manifest), the discoverer of things, the comprehender of things, and it precedes the creation of all things and follows the existence of all things, as it is said, 'God is the Light of the Heaven and Earth' (Quran).
But the light of Intuition (or Inner Perception) is a light which comprehends the realities and the core of things.

order.why: Read a reported generalization about intuition in its own setting.
Bring inward and outward attention together.
Pair reliance on intuition with an admission of error.
Widen guidance beyond inspiration alone.
Hold prayer and effort together with fallibility.
Consider the difficulty of interpreting visions.
Encounter a distinct philosophical account of direct knowledge.
Connect receptivity with contemplation of evidence.
Retain the ocean image with its supplied citation.

questions: What could help you distinguish a fruitful intuition from a wish, a fear, or an inherited assumption?
How do the cautions about inspiration alter the way you read the more confident descriptions of inward perception?
What roles might prayer, consultation, evidence, and subsequent experience each play in testing an impression?
How can a community welcome unusual insights while making it easy for people to revise their judgments?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the inmost heart as a measure of understanding.
Connect inward discernment with the responsibility to see and hear for oneself.

references.label: 1 · 1 Thessalonians 5:19–22 — receptivity and testing
references.note: Paul places openness to the Spirit beside the instruction to examine what is received and retain what is good. Compare that pairing with the compilation’s simultaneous encouragement of inward perception and warnings about error. The Christian setting also invites inquiry into what each tradition understands spiritual inspiration to be.

subjects.introduction: In a dream we see without eyes and travel without moving our feet. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá takes that ordinary strangeness seriously, distinguishing the visions of the Prophets from confused dreaming and describing a spirit that operates with or without bodily instruments. Bahá’u’lláh calls sleep a world among the divine worlds, evidence of a realm without beginning or end, and allows that it may be named the world of similitudes between spirit and matter, where whatever exists in heaven or on earth has its counterpart. Later Sufi philosophers mapped that intermediate region as a barzakh of luminous substance, neither body nor pure intellect, with cities of its own; modern scholars read their accounts with care, and these voices should be kept distinct from the Bahá’í texts. Plato’s divided line, with its visible figures that help the mind think beyond them, offers a different way of asking what an image can do [1]. The path continues into the importance of dreams and visions, the power of imagination, and the isthmus that joins and separates the worlds.
subjects.arc: Start with spiritual discovery expressed as vision, then explore how different authors understand images and intermediate realities.

order.why: Establish the distinction between spiritual discovery and ordinary dreaming.
shortened: In like manner, spiritual disclosures are of two kinds. One is the visions of the Prophets and the spiritual disclosures of the chosen ones of God. The visions of the Prophets are not dreams but true spiritual disclosures. Thus when they say, "I saw someone in such a form, and I spoke such words, and he gave such a reply", this vision takes place in a state of wakefulness and not in the realm of sleep. It is a spiritual discovery that is expressed in the form of a vision.

order.why: Explicitly identifies a world of exemplars as the heavenly body of man, then explains the distinction between the bodily self and the reality with which one inwardly consults.
Consider the soul’s activity apart from outward sensation.
Encounter the varied accounts of dreams and their sources.
shortened: Likewise, a question was asked concerning sleep. It is a special world among the divine worlds and is indicative of infinite matters. Among other things, it is evidence of a realm wherein no beginning or end, no first or last, can be witnessed. Thus, something is observed in sleep, and after a number of years that very same thing is witnessed. If it be said that this is the world of similitudes between the two worlds - which some consider to be a semi-spiritual realm between the worlds of spirit and matter - this would be correct.
Sleep sometimes varies according to the differences in souls, thoughts, food and drink. In the dreams of holy souls there hath been and is no variation, for they are pure wakefulness.

order.why: Compare remembering a vision with recalling a journey.
shortened: An observant traveller passing along a way will certainly recall his discoveries to mind, unless some accident befall him and efface the memory.

order.why: Explore spiritual meanings appearing in bodily forms.
Introduce counterparts between hidden and manifest worlds.
shortened: The meaning of the Kingdom (malakut) in its primary sense and degree is the scene of His transcendent glory. In another sense it is the world of similitudes ('alam-i-mithal) which existeth between the Dominion on high (jabarut) and this mortal realm (nasut); whatever is in the heavens or on the earth hath its counterpart in that world. Whilst a thing remaineth hidden and concealed within the power of utterance it is said to be of the Dominion (jabarut), and this is the first stage of its substantiation (taqyid). Whenever it becometh manifest it is said to be of the Kingdom (malakut).

order.why: Read a scholar’s definition of an intermediate realm.
Hear the older philosophical account quoted within that discussion.
shortened: Know that the 'alam-i-mithal is a spiritual universe of luminous substance; on the one hand it has an affinity with material substance, in that it is the object of perception and possesses extent; on the other hand, it has an affinity with separate intelligible substance, in that its nature is that of pure light. It is neither a compound material body, nor a separate intelligible substance, because it is a barzakh, that is, an interworld, a limit, which separates the one from the other.

order.why: Examine the more elaborate landscape of the imaginal world.
shortened: So here we have a threefold universe: an intelligible universe, a sensory universe, and between the two a universe for which it is difficult in our language to find a satisfactory term.... So this is a universe which symbolizes both with corporeal substance, because it possesses shape, dimensions, and extent - and with separated or intelligible substance, because it is essentially made of light (nurani). It is both immaterial matter and the incorporeal corporealized. It is the limit which separates and at the same time unites them.

order.why: Close with a distinct philosophical interpretation of dream and reality.

questions: What differences do you notice among a dream, a symbol, a spiritual discovery, and an imagined scene?
When can treating an image literally obscure what it communicates, and when can a symbolic reading become too unconstrained?
How do the Bahá’í passages and the philosophical commentaries differ in the claims they make about images?
What kinds of reflection or evidence would help you interpret a powerful inward experience responsibly?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the acknowledged difficulty of distinguishing and interpreting visions.
Explore the image of the sun and mirror in accounts of the soul.

references.label: 1 · Plato, Republic VI, 509d–511e — images and understanding
references.note: In the divided line, Plato distinguishes images, visible objects, and forms of intellectual understanding; even geometry uses visible figures to think beyond them. Compare this account with the compilation’s intermediate world of images. The schemes are different: a comparison can clarify the work an image performs without identifying their categories.

subjects.introduction: Sunlight reaches the earth without the sun ever leaving its place in the sky, while a flower grows out of a tree by the tree’s own substance unfolding into it. Between those two pictures lies a question that ‘Abdu’l-Bahá returns to again and again: how can everything that exists depend wholly on God without being a piece of God? He answers that creation emanates from its Source as rays from the sun, as speech from a speaker, as a letter from the hand that writes it; the Source remains sanctified above what proceeds from it, and nothing of the divine Essence is divided or descends. Aquinas, examining creation as the dependence of all being upon its universal cause, gives the question a kindred philosophical shape [1]. To think this way is to learn nearness without confusion and transcendence without distance. The path continues toward the Primal Will through which all things are called into being, toward the station of the Manifestation of God, and toward the ceaseless, all-pervading bounty by which the outpouring never stops.
subjects.arc: Begin with two familiar forms of dependence, test their implications, and distinguish a created effect from a division of the divine essence.

order.why: Develop the contrast through seed and branches. Locate the disagreement described in the philosophical text. Close with unity of source without alteration of that source.
shortened: The difference resides in the fact that the Sufis maintain that the realities of all things are the manifestation of the One, whereas the Prophets say that they emanate therefrom.

For example, when the seed, which is a single thing endowed with the perfections of the vegetable kingdom, manifests itself, it becomes resolved into the infinite forms of the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit. This is called manifestational appearance, whereas in appearance through emanation the One remains transcendent in the heights of its sanctity, but the existence of the creatures is obtained from it through emanation, not manifestation. It can be compared to the sun: The rays emanate from it and shine forth upon all things, but the sun remains transcendent in the heights of its sanctity.

order.why: Open with the vivid difference between flower and sunlight.
shortened: And the realization of things is of two kinds: manifestational and emanational. The manifestational is like when a flower emerges from this tree - this is manifestational realization. But what we mean is emanational realization, like rays emanating from the sun.

order.why: Ask what transformation would imply about the divine source. Connect dependence with a quickening spiritual influence.
shortened: This quickening spirit emanates spontaneously from the Sun of Truth, from the reality of Divinity, and is not a revelation or a manifestation. It is like the rays of the sun. The rays are emanations from the sun.
This plant beside me has risen from the seed; therefore, it is a manifestation and unfoldment of the seed.
But the reality of Divinity is indivisible, and each individual of humankind cannot be a part of it as is often claimed.

order.why: Clarify the seed image in the fuller philosophical discussion. Introduce speech as an alternative model of dependence. Return to the speaker without treating speech as a severed part.
shortened: Now, just as the writing emanates from the writer and the discourse from the speaker, so does the human spirit emanate from God. But it does not manifest Him: that is, no part has been separated from the divine Reality to enter into the body of man. No, the human spirit has emanated, just as speech emanates from the speaker, and become manifested in the body of man.

As for manifestational procession, it is the manifestation of the reality of a thing in other forms, like the procession of this tree or this flower from their seeds, for it is the seed itself that has become manifested in the form of the branches, leaves and flowers.

order.why: Examine why change creates a difficulty for this analogy. Compare creation with an artisan’s work. Make the indivisibility of the divine essence explicit.
shortened: Answer: The connection between God and His creation is that of the originator and the originated, of the sun and the dark bodies of the universe, of the craftsman and his handiwork.

But appearance through manifestation is like the manifestation of the branches, leaves, blossoms and fruits from the seed; for the seed itself becomes the branches and fruit and its reality descends into them. This manifestational appearance would be sheer imperfection and utterly impossible for the Most High, for this would require unconditioned pre-existence to take on the attributes of the originated, absolute independence to become abject poverty, and the essence of existence to become pure non-existence; and this is in no wise possible.

order.why: Hold together origin in God and distinction from God.
shortened: But the people of truth maintain that the appearance of the realities of things from the True One is through emanation, not manifestation, just as the ray emanates from luminous bodies - all are from Him but are not Him. The luminous rays, infinite bounties, and spiritual impressions and reflections emanated from the Sun of Truth; it is not that they were the manifestation of the Sun of Truth.

order.why: Revisit the difference between transformation and origination. Hear the contrast stated in another reported account.
Distinguish the Manifestation and the radiance of the Spirit.
shortened: Question: "And whosoever speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the world to come."

Answer: The sanctified realities of the Manifestations of God have two spiritual stations: One is that of the state of divine manifestation, which can be compared to the orb of the sun, and the other is that of radiance and revelation, which may be likened to the divine light and perfections--the Holy Spirit.

order.why: Explicitly distinguishes dependence by emanation from manifestation, incarnation and acquisition.
Read the reported clarification concerning prophetic reflection.
shortened: The Prophet is the emanation (radiation) of the Eternal Light. It is not an emanation of substance, but an overflowing, a reflection (literally: reflect, throw back) of light and warmth. All things appertaining to prophethood are a manifestation, a reflection of the Divine."

order.why: Consider the reported image of rays.

questions: Which features of the sun, speech, and seed analogies help explain dependence, and where does each analogy become misleading?
What changes if creation is understood as transformation of a substance rather than an effect of a source?
How do these passages hold divine transcendence together with the nearness of divine influence?
What distinctions become necessary when the word “manifestation” appears in different settings?

neighbors.invitation: Apply the speaker-and-speech analogy to the origin of the soul.
Consider why matter and form are described as inseparable in created things.

references.label: 1 · Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, question 45, article 1 — creation and cause
references.note: Aquinas distinguishes creation, understood as the dependence of all being on a universal cause, from changes that presuppose existing material. Read this alongside the compilation’s distinction between emanation and transformation. Compare the arguments carefully rather than assuming that a shared word carries an identical philosophical system.

subjects.introduction: Where does a soul come from, and when does it begin? ‘Abdu’l-Bahá answers with the image of speech: the human spirit issues from God as words issue from a speaker, wholly dependent on its source yet never a piece broken off from it. The soul is a divine emanation, a breath of the All-Merciful, a ray of the Sun of Reality shining in the mirror of the body. Each soul, the Writings explain, has a real beginning, at conception, and once begun it never ends; talk of a prior existence points to potentiality, not to a person who remembers another life. The Preacher of Ecclesiastes saw the dust return to the earth and the spirit return to its Giver [1], and the Bahá’í teachings carry that thought further, toward an existence of endless progress. To ponder this beginning is to approach the relationship of the soul to the body, its immaterial and undying nature, and the all-pervading bounty of God from which every life flows.
subjects.arc: Explore the soul’s dependence on its source, examine different uses of preexistence, and read the later clarifications before returning to spiritual identity.

order.why: Develop the image of speech issuing from a speaker.
shortened: No, the human spirit has emanated, just as speech emanates from the speaker, and become manifested in the body of man.

order.why: Begin by distinguishing the soul from bodily composition.
Explains that the rational soul does not subsist through the body and possesses individuality from the beginning.
Consider the growth of capacity during embodied life.
Hear the soul’s origin expressed as a divine breath.
shortened: It is evident that the human soul is the breaths of the All-Merciful, and the spirit of life is the divine inspirations of the All-Loving God.

order.why: Attend to the terminology of a reported conversation.
Encounter the question of souls before bodily existence.
Distinguish potentiality from individual consciousness. Revisit potentiality in the separately supplied selection.
Place a beginning alongside the soul’s enduring existence.
Read prayerful language of eternity in its own voice.
Preserve the source’s question without inventing its absent answer.
Explore origin and reflection through sun and mirror.
Consider the reported language of spiritual confirmation.
shortened: Thus it is proven that man is man through his spirit, not his body. This spirit is an effusion of divine bounties, a ray from the Sun of Reality. But if this human spirit is confirmed by the breaths of the Holy Spirit, then it becomes the true spirit, and the breaths of the Holy Spirit are the divine teachings. Then it attains eternal life, acquires heavenly illumination, and enlightens the human world with divine virtues.

order.why: End with the tension between divine likeness and distinct identity.
shortened: Look with the eye of thy heart: thy reality is the Lordship of thy Lord for thee through thee - thou art He and He is thou, except that thou art thou and He is He. He has a station of unity, His identity is pure essence - no mention, no indication, no expression of this station except through inability, and this is the perfection of unity through negation of attributes and Lordship, which when there is no object of Lordship has no mention, no encompassing, no manifestation.

order.why: Introduce later guidance on beginning and endless progress.
Read the explicit clarification concerning conception.
Follow with the corresponding explanation from the House of Justice.
Resolve the specific question about individual preexistence.

questions: How do the passages distinguish dependence on God from being a part of God?
What different meanings can “preexistence” carry, and how do the later clarifications help sort them out?
How does the image of a life with a beginning and unending progress alter the way you think about present capacities?
What does careful reading require when a prayer, a reported conversation, and an explanatory letter use related terms differently?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the philosophical distinction underlying the image of speech and speaker.
Consider a further account of spiritual identity through the inmost heart.

references.label: 1 · Ecclesiastes 12:1–7 — dust and spirit
references.note: Ecclesiastes places the return of spirit to God within a poetic meditation on aging and mortality. Compare its movement from bodily frailty toward origin with the compilation’s accounts of the soul. The passage invites reflection on dependence and return without itself settling the question of when an individual soul begins.

subjects.introduction: A seed is sown, disappears into stem and leaf and fruit, and at the end seeds appear again; are they the same seed? ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses that homely puzzle to open the question of what persists when things change. Bahá’u’lláh offers another clue in ink and letters: the ink exists before any letter is written and could take any shape, the shape exists in the writer’s mind before it touches paper, yet neither can appear in the world without the other. Matter and form can be told apart in thought and never in the thing, which is close to what Aristotle found when he asked whether nature is the underlying stuff or the defining shape [1]. Around this centre very different voices gather: the Báb’s symbolic account of Will and Purpose as father and mother of all things, the Sufi debate over whether existence is a substance or an accident of the mind, alchemical descriptions of a subtle substance filling all interstices, and reported remarks about atoms in the vocabulary of their time. None of it is modern physics, and the fairest question to ask of each is what kind of explanation it offers. The path continues into the indestructibility of elementary matter, the law of transformation and change, the four elements, and the uncompounded reality beneath them all.
subjects.arc: Begin with continuity through change, explore the interdependence of matter and form, and leave the source’s research questions open for further inquiry.

order.why: Develop matter and form through the vivid image of written letters.
shortened: For example it has been stated that all things are composed of two elements:  the "Fashioner" [qabil] and the "Fashioned" [maqbul].  By "Fashioned" is meant substance [madda] and primary matter [huyula] and by "Fashioner" is meant the form and shape which confines and limits the primary matter from its state of indefiniteness and freedom to the courtyard of limitation and definite form.  For example, letters and words are composed of two things:  The first is the substance which is ink and pencil-lead and is the "Fashioned" while the second is the forms and features of the letters and words which are the "Fashioner".

For it is not possible for a thing to have an external existence and not to be formed into a shape because substance and primal matter in order to exist need shape and form; while shape and form in order to appear need substance.

order.why: Open with the difference between a returning quality and an identical thing.
Consider the relation of matter and form through a familiar light.
shortened: The sun is born of matter and form, which can be likened to father and mother, and still it is absolute perfection; darkness has neither matter nor form, neither father nor mother, and yet it is sheer imperfection.

order.why: Widen change into the interconnected life of existence.
Explore varied names and stages of one reality.
Read the reported account of atoms in its historical vocabulary.
shortened: Matter, the corporeal, consists of atoms which are alike; they, the atoms, fill up space, they are units without magnitude conceived as points, on which all spatial corporeal existence is based. The atoms do not penetrate into each other, they move, they change.

order.why: Explains the differentiation of matter into elements and the formation of beings through their combination.
Consider the Báb’s symbolic account of willing and forming.
shortened: The Kaf is the rank of the Primal Will, and the Nun is the rank of Purpose, and the Primal Will is the father of all things and Purpose their mother.

Through the Kaf God created the substance of things and the sign of His uniqueness and the temple of His oneness, indicating God alone, and it is the highest consciousness in contingency wherein God alone is known, and it is called the heart. Through the Nun God created things from the beginning of inclination toward Himself to the uttermost multiplicity, from infinity unto infinity.

order.why: Clarify the distinction between substance and a mental abstraction.
shortened: For the generality of the Sufis understand by "Existence" that common existence which is conceived by the mind and intellect of man; that is, which man can comprehend.
This common existence, however, is only one accident among others that enter upon the realities of created things, while the essences of beings are the substance.

Now, the substance is undoubtedly superior to the accident, for the substance is primary and the accident secondary; the substance subsists through itself while the accident subsists through something else; that is, it needs a substance through which it can subsist.

order.why: Compare another account of that philosophical distinction.
shortened: Those pre-eminent Sufis who founded the doctrine of the "unity of existence" never intended by this term the universally predicated existence which is conceived by the mind. For such an existence is but an accident among others occurring in association with the realities of things. That is to say, these realities are the substance, whereas that existence which is conceived by the mind, the universally predicated existence, is but an accident associated with them.

order.why: Return to the search for constancy behind changing appearances.
Distinguish ink, form, and the movement that writes.
Encounter a scholar’s account of substance in Ibn Arabi.
Read the historical alchemical description in its own terms.
shortened: As for jawhar, God protect you, it is the one thing by which the interstices are filled (al-mamlu' bihi al-khalal). It is capable of taking any form. Everything is in it, everything is constituted out of it, and everything dissolves back to it.
This is the body which is in all three kingdoms of nature, namely animals, plants and stones....

order.why: Explore the language of active and receptive principles.
Connect substance with the imagery of heat and the Word.
Consider a reported relation between matter and spirit.
Read the reference to invisible forces without imposing modern equations.

questions: What remains continuous when a thing changes its form, and how do the seed and writing analogies answer differently?
Which passages offer metaphysical explanations, which use spiritual images, and which preserve questions for research?
What becomes clearer when matter and form are distinguished, and what becomes misleading if they are treated as entirely independent?
How could a conversation between these texts and contemporary science respect the different questions each is equipped to address?

neighbors.invitation: Explore active and receptive principles alongside the image of a life-giving Word.
Consider a kind of dependence that does not require a shared material substance.

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Physics II.1 — matter and form
references.note: Aristotle examines both underlying material and defining form when asking what nature is. His examples distinguish a thing’s potential from its actuality. Compare this with the compilation’s ink and letters: what can be separated in an explanation that cannot be separated in the concrete thing? Keep this philosophical comparison distinct from a claim about current physics.

subjects.introduction: The world came into being, Bahá’u’lláh writes, through the heat generated between an active force and its recipient, and in the same breath He asks His reader to be a throbbing artery in the body of creation, so that the heat of that motion may quicken hesitant hearts. Heat and motion do several kinds of work. They belong to an older natural philosophy in which lightness rises because of warmth and stillness comes from cold; they describe the perpetual movement of atoms and the test of life itself; and they become images of a fire latent in wood, or in a heart, waiting for the force that will release it. Aristotle, asking whether fire alone can account for a living thing’s growth and finding that organized form needs another explanation [1], is a useful partner from a neighbouring ancient account. Bahá’u’lláh sets His heat above the kinds in the books of men, because it proceeds from the Word. The path leads on to the four elements, to love as fire, and to the teaching that all things are in motion.
subjects.arc: Begin with creation and the quickening heart, distinguish the uses of heat and motion, and return to the Word as a source of activity.

order.why: Open with cosmic activity turning toward the human heart. Read the fuller account of active and receptive principles.
shortened: The world of existence came into being through the heat generated from the interaction between the active force and that which is its recipient. These two are the same, yet they are different. Thus doth the Great Announcement inform thee about this glorious structure. Such as communicate the generating influence and such as receive its impact are indeed created through the irresistible Word of God which is the Cause of the entire creation, while all else besides His Word are but the creatures and the effects thereof.
Be thou as a throbbing artery, pulsating in the body of the entire creation, that through the heat generated by this motion there may appear that which will quicken the hearts of those who hesitate.

order.why: Connect latent force with the warmth of spiritual love.
shortened: Heat exists in all things, but a force is needed to make it manifest. Likewise in the world of religion, the power of Baha'u'llah makes manifest the heat of the love of God - that is, the latent power hidden in hearts - and expands the sphere of thoughts, bestows enlightenment, and shows the path of guidance.

order.why: Explore motion as a feature of living existence.
Consider the reported image of fire latent in wood.
Enter the historical vocabulary of heat and ascent.
Hear another expression of the relation between heat and rising.
shortened: O friend! The cause of motion is heat, and the cause of ascension is lightness. God willing, the fire of the love of God which is deposited in thy verses will become the cause of ascension and the reason for motion, and will unite the friends with the friends.

order.why: Notice an explicit distinction from familiar accounts of heat.
Explicitly connects motion with heat within an explanation of the four elements.
Consider stillness and motion through the energies of the Word.
Retain the brief comparison of heat and differing effects. Close with the source’s combined selection on spiritual warmth.
Distinguish several kinds of motion.
Widen attention to the movement of atoms.
Connect the language of substance with the Word.
Return to the Word as the cause described in the text.
Encounter the extended historical account of cosmic formation.
Consider heat as an image of concentrated activity.
Preserve the separately supplied provisional rendering.

questions: Where do heat and motion function as descriptions of nature, and where do they become spiritual images?
What does the image of a hidden fire suggest about capacities that have not yet become visible?
How might the account of creation shape the way these passages describe a word’s effect on a person?
What questions should we ask before translating the vocabulary of historical natural philosophy into contemporary scientific terms?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the related language of substance, heat, and the Word.
Consider the power attributed to a word that imparts new life.

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, On the Soul II.4 — fire and living growth
references.note: Aristotle asks whether fire explains nutrition and growth, then argues that a living thing’s organized limits require another kind of explanation. Compare the roles assigned to heat, activity, and form in these passages. This is a conversation between historical accounts of nature, with a further question about how their images become spiritually suggestive.

subjects.displayTitle: The capacity of every human being
subjects.introduction: A compass needle far from the pole swings toward it, while the rock lying at the pole feels nothing. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s image shifts the question of spiritual recognition from distance to receptivity, and the Bahá’í writings answer it generously: every human being has been made able, of himself, to appreciate the beauty of God, and no one will be excused on the plea that everybody else turned away. Yet the flame is latent in the candle and the light in the lamp, and neither can kindle itself; the mirror cannot clear its own dust. Upbringing, vain imaginings, effort and help from others all bear on whether a capacity becomes a life, and the Manifestation of God is the fire that lights the wick. Mencius placed compassion, shame and discernment in everyone while admitting how often they go unreflected upon [1], a confidence worth setting beside this account of cultivation and grace. The journey continues toward the development of capacity through education, toward the bounty and mercy of God that reach every soul, and toward the oneness of humanity that such confidence demands.
subjects.arc: Awaken curiosity through a compass and an unlit candle, explore the conditions of growth, and conclude with a community spacious enough for everyone.

order.why: Consider the human being as a gem of distinctive capacity.
Turn potential into the familiar image of an unlit candle.
Begin with a compass responding where a nearby stone cannot.
Connect human distinction with spiritual virtues.
Explore the range of human faculties.
Relate recognition to signs and words.
shortened: Say: The first and foremost testimony establishing His truth is His own Self. Next to this testimony is His Revelation. For whoso faileth to recognize either the one or the other He hath established the words He hath revealed as proof of His reality and truth. This is, verily, an evidence of His tender mercy unto men. He hath endowed every soul with the capacity to recognize the signs of God.

order.why: Ask what happens when available faculties go unused.
shortened: This humble servant is filled with wonder, inasmuch as all men are endowed with the capacity to see and hear, yet we find them deprived of the privilege of using these faculties.

order.why: Examine how upbringing and assumptions can obstruct understanding.
shortened: It is most clear that every soul has been and will be a seeker after the knowledge of God, and the cause of rejection, objection, heedlessness and ignorance has been the vain imaginings with which they were formerly raised.

order.why: Distinguish potential receptivity from readiness for a particular trust.
shortened: Not every heart is capable of acting as a repository for divine love. For not every soul is suited for growing wondrous herbs--only the heart of a human being who continues to bear the trustworthiness of the All-Merciful and to give the fruit of wisdom and eloquence.

order.why: Bring cultivation into view through the sapling heart.
shortened: Behold how the generality of mankind hath been endued with the capacity to hearken unto God's most exalted Word - the Word upon which must depend the gathering together and spiritual resurrection of all men.

The Word of God may be likened unto a sapling, whose roots have been implanted in the hearts of men. It is incumbent upon you to foster its growth through the living waters of wisdom, of sanctified and holy words, so that its root may become firmly fixed and its branches may spread out as high as the heavens and beyond.

order.why: Allow growth to unfold gradually.
shortened: Similarly, in the contingent world, the human species hath undergone progressive physical changes and, by a slow process, hath scaled the ladder of civilization, realizing in itself the wonders, excellencies and gifts of humanity in their most glorious form, until it gained the capacity to express the splendours of spiritual perfections and divine ideals and became capable of hearkening to the call of God.

order.why: Consider equality through turning toward a shared source.
Hear the reach of grace beyond a privileged few.
shortened: The grace of the True One hath been and shall ever be vouchsafed unto all, and He hath summoned all with one call to the supreme horizon.

order.why: Reinforce the breadth of divine bounty.
shortened: The breaths of the verses have encompassed all created things, and they have been sent down at all times from the presence of the All-Merciful. Blessed is the soul that hath inhaled them and circled round them! Were the peoples of the East and West to purify their ears, they would hear them, and thy Lord is verily a witness unto what I say. This bounty is not confined to anyone, but hath encompassed all worlds. Blessed is he who hath turned unto Him, and woe betide them that have turned aside!

order.why: Affirms that love of the divine verses is created in every heart and invites all to hear and acknowledge them.
Connect shared capacity with understanding and wisdom.
shortened: The True One, exalted be His glory, hath created all mankind for His knowledge, and hath adorned all with the ornament of understanding and wisdom, that none might be deprived of the living waters which are the recognition of the All-Merciful.

order.why: Place the search for knowledge within creation’s purpose.
shortened: Reflect a little: the whole world hath been created for the knowledge of God. In all the heavenly Books, they were given the glad-tidings of the Most Great Manifestation.

order.why: Read a reported encounter concerning recognition across cultures.
Preserve the individual’s responsibility to investigate.
shortened: It followeth, therefore, that every man hath been, and will continue to be, able of himself to appreciate the Beauty of God, the Glorified. Had he not been endowed with such a capacity, how could he be called to account for his failure? If, in the Day when all the peoples of the earth will be gathered together, any man should, whilst standing in the presence of God, be asked: “Wherefore hast thou disbelieved in My Beauty and turned away from My Self?”, and if such a man should reply and say: “Inasmuch as all men have erred, and none hath been found willing to turn his face to the Truth, I, too, following their example, have grievously failed to recognize the Beauty of the Eternal,” such a plea will, assuredly, be rejected.

order.why: Ask why a candle and mirror still need assistance. Consider teachings as a means of releasing potential. Return to knowing and loving as a human purpose.
shortened: Having created the world and all that liveth and moveth therein, He, through the direct operation of His unconstrained and sovereign Will, chose to confer upon man the unique distinction and capacity to know Him and to love Him -- a capacity that must needs be regarded as the generating impulse and the primary purpose underlying the whole of creation, as mentioned in the well-known sacred tradition.

These energies with which the Daystar of Divine bounty and Source of heavenly guidance hath endowed the reality of man lie, however, latent within him, even as the flame is hidden within the candle and the rays of light are potentially present in the lamp. The radiance of these energies may be obscured by worldly desires even as the light of the sun can be concealed beneath the dust and dross which cover the mirror. Neither the candle nor the lamp can be lighted through their own unaided efforts, nor can it ever be possible for the mirror to free itself from its dross. It is clear and evident that until a fire is kindled the lamp will never be ignited, and unless the dross is blotted out from the face of the mirror it can never represent the image of the sun nor reflect its light and glory.

order.why: End with the practical invitation to make room for all.

questions: How can equal spiritual worth coexist with differences in developed capacities and present circumstances?
What do the compass, candle, gem, and sapling each reveal about growth?
Where do personal effort and assistance from others meet in the development of a capacity?
How would confidence in everyone’s possibilities change the way a community welcomes, educates, and shares responsibility?

neighbors.invitation: Connect the exercise of human capacities with seeing and hearing independently.
Consider the preparation of the heart as a place of receptivity.

references.label: 1 · Mencius, Gaozi I.6 — shared moral capacities
references.note: Mencius argues that compassion, shame, respect, and moral discernment belong to human nature, although people may fail to reflect on them. Compare this confidence with the compilation’s images of capacities needing cultivation. Explore the different accounts of moral development and of the assistance needed to bring a possibility into action.

subjects.introduction: God has made death a door to His grace, Bahá’u’lláh writes, and most people do not know it. Everything composed must one day decompose; the ant, the mountain, and the star each have a lifetime, and no one escapes the messenger when he comes. But the Writings use the words life and death in more than one sense. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes a death that is appointed from one that proper care might have averted, and then speaks of a death of the heart that can afflict the outwardly living, which is what Christ meant when He let the dead bury their dead. Measured against the life of the Kingdom, the mineral’s life is death, and so is any existence turned away from its source. John’s Gospel sets the same present passing from death to life beside a resurrection still to come [1]. Such language is for self-examination, not for sentencing others. It opens onto the living waters that quicken a soul, onto the cycles of composition and decomposition that run through creation, and onto the distance between the ephemeral and the eternal.
subjects.arc: Begin with death as a doorway, acknowledge bodily mortality, and then explore the different meanings of becoming spiritually alive.

order.why: Consider lifetimes across very different scales of existence.
Open the difficult subject with the image of a door to grace.
Ground the discussion in composition and dissolution.
shortened: Since the foundation of life, through divine power, is the connection and combination of these essences, inevitably one day it must change to separation and dissolution must occur. Therefore no soul has deliverance from death, and none can find escape from this whirlpool of mortality.

order.why: Introduce the distinction between conditional and inevitable death.
Keep care and prayer within that distinction.
shortened: Regarding what thou hadst written about reciting prayers with complete confidence for the healing of those friends, and then their passing occurring - know that there are two kinds of destined time of death: one is the inevitable destined time, and the other is the suspended destined time. These prayers, supplications, pleading, seeking of healing and protection are for preservation from the suspended destined time, not from the appointed and inevitable time. Otherwise, no soul would hasten from this mortal world to the eternal realm, for whenever someone falls ill, either they themselves would pray or others would pray for them and they would be healed.

order.why: Acknowledge the limit no one escapes.
Ask what earthly possessions can finally provide.
shortened: Will anything on earth profit anyone when death overtaketh him? Nay, by the Lord of all worlds! Blessed is he unto whom death is the ultimate annihilation and the beginning of his immortality through God, the Almighty, the Help in Peril, the Self-Subsisting.

order.why: Introduce spiritual life through a particular example.
Explore the relativity of life across levels of existence.
Distinguish spiritual comparison from annihilation.
shortened: The meaning of Christ's saying was not that the unbelievers become absolutely annihilated; the meaning of Christ is that the life of those, who reject Him is as non-existent, compared with the life of those who accept Him.

order.why: Read the expression about the dead burying the dead.
Turn from temporary bodily restoration toward enduring transformation.
shortened: These outward miracles are of no importance to the followers of truth. For example, if a blind man is made to see, in the end he will again lose his sight, for he will die and be deprived of all his senses and faculties. Thus, causing the blind to see is of no lasting importance, since the faculty of sight is bound to be lost again in the end. And if a dead body be revived, what is gained thereby, since it must die again?

order.why: Encounter the fountain as an image of life.
Consider the meaning of spiritual deadness.
Connect resurrection with awakening.
Relate life to turning toward its source.
shortened: Every soul who today turns to the Luminary of the horizon of inner meanings is accounted among the living before the Divine Countenance, and whoso remains deprived is reckoned among the dead.

order.why: Hear the promise of enduring spiritual life.
Ask what prevents a person from drinking.
shortened: Whoso draweth nigh and drinketh, verily he is of the people of Baha before God, the Lord of Names; and whoso is debarred, he is assuredly among the dead.

order.why: Consider remembrance that outlasts bodily existence.
shortened: And whoso hath attained unto this, verily he liveth in Our exalted Kingdom and his mention shall endure through the eternity of God, the Lord of the worlds. And whoso is deprived, he is indeed among the dead though he be among those who speak.

order.why: Preserve the supplied summary and its lamp image.
shortened: Its eventual extinction is therefore certain and it is impossible to change or alter this outcome, for such is its irrevocable fate. Likewise, a power has been created in the body of man whose depletion and exhaustion leads inevitably to the disintegration of the body. It is even as the oil in this lamp: after it has been burnt and consumed, the lamp will assuredly be extinguished.

order.why: Read the Báb’s account of death and life.
shortened: Say: God provideth sustenance to every soul, and verily He is the Provider, the Most Exalted, the All-Powerful, the Impregnable, the Possessor of might and majesty. Say: Who causeth all things to die and then giveth them life? Say: God, more swiftly than to say "Be" and it is. Such is God, your Lord. His is the creation and the command. There is no God but Him, the Mighty, the Beloved.

order.why: Distinguishes bodily existence from spiritual life and explains the relative use of life and death.
Explore the association between ignorance and spiritual death.
Close with a challenging passage on hesitation and recognition.

questions: How does the meaning of life or death change from one passage to another?
What practices might make life more awake, receptive, and generous in the present?
How can spiritual language about death deepen self-examination without diminishing compassion for others?
What does mortality reveal about the difference between what we possess, what we do, and what may endure?

neighbors.invitation: Explore a life with a beginning and the prospect of endless progress.
Consider spiritual transformation through changes in character and outward conditions.

references.label: 1 · John 5:24–29 — life now and resurrection
references.note: John places a present passage from death to life beside an account of those in graves hearing the Son’s voice. Compare the temporal and spiritual meanings within the Gospel passage with the compilation’s several uses of life and death. What does each reading connect to hearing, response, and conduct?

subjects.introduction: Persians need not become Bahá’ís, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá said; let them simply act on Bahá’u’lláh’s teachings and watch what happens. An age can be transformed before anyone agrees on what is transforming it. The teachings He called the spirit of this age and the light of this century are measured by their effects: quarrelsome factions turned to peace, independent inquiry replacing blind imitation, the oneness of humanity, the harmony of science and religion, freedom from prejudice; and Bahá’u’lláh Himself speaks of a new life breathed into every human frame and a fresh potency instilled in every word. Jesus, noting that people can read the sky for rain yet cannot read their own time, asked them to judge for themselves what is right [1]; discernment of an age is a form of attention, not a taste for novelty. The most hopeful image is the bird of the love of God spreading its wings over every horizon, for the remedy and the renewal are finally the same thing, love. The way leads on to the greatness of this Day and to the spiritual springtime.
subjects.arc: Look first for teachings in practice, examine the needs of a changing world, and end with renewal expressed through love.

order.why: Challenge the habit of blind imitation.
Make the change concrete through conflict turned toward peace.
shortened: After Our arrival, We revealed, as a copious rain, by the aid of God and His Divine Grace and mercy, Our verses, and sent them to various parts of the world. We exhorted all men, and particularly this people, through Our wise counsels and loving admonitions, and forbade them to engage in sedition, quarrels, disputes and conflict. As a result of this, and by the grace of God, waywardness and folly were changed into piety and understanding, and weapons converted into instruments of peace.

order.why: Set out principles by which a new spirit might be recognized.
shortened: At such a time as this Baha'u'llah proclaimed the first principle of His mission and teaching -- the oneness of the world of humanity. His second announcement was the investigation of reality; the third was the oneness of the foundations of the divine religions. Through spiritual education He led the people out of darkness and ignorance into the clear light of truth, illuminated their hearts with the splendor of knowledge, laid a true and universal basis for religious teachings, cultivated the virtues of humanity, conferred spiritual susceptibilities, awakened inner perceptions and changed the dishonor of prejudiced souls to the highest degree of honor and capacity.

order.why: Consider teachings as nourishment for humanity.
Let the language of keys suggest newly opened understanding.
Connect the pen with the spread of teachings.
Retain the brief expression of the age’s spirit.
Lists teachings explicitly described as the spirit of the age and connects them with practice and the Covenant.
Judge religious vitality through its fruits.
shortened: The sacred Manifestations were not known in the first cycles and the fruit of their mission had not been discovered. But in this spiritual age, in this divine time the exaltation and the luminosity, the truth and the greatness of the Cause of God have become manifest and evident as the sun in all regions. All wise men witness that these divine teachings are the very spirit of this age, and the light of this cycle; humanity will never find peace and tranquillity without the spreading of these teachings, nor will it attain perfect civilization.

order.why: Bring the search for a remedy back to love.
shortened: Meanwhile, the supreme antidote and the instantaneous cure for the ills of the people of the world are the sacred teachings of the Ancient Beauty (may my spirit be sacrificed for His loved ones) and true love for that heart-ravishing countenance.

order.why: Hear the creative potency attributed to the Word.
shortened: Through the movement of Our Pen of glory We have, at the bidding of the omnipotent Ordainer, breathed a new life into every human frame, and instilled into every word a fresh potency. All created things proclaim the evidences of this world-wide regeneration.

order.why: Consider the announcement of a new creation.
shortened: This is the Day whereon naught can be seen except the splendors of the Light that shineth from the face of Thy Lord, the Gracious, the Most Bountiful. Verily, We have caused every soul to expire by virtue of Our irresistible and all-subduing sovereignty. We have, then, called into being a new creation, as a token of Our grace unto men.

order.why: Place the new utterance within a wider prophetic horizon.
shortened: This is the Ocean out of which all seas have proceeded, and with which every one of them will ultimately be united. From Him all the Suns have been generated, and unto Him they will all return. Through His potency the Trees of Divine Revelation have yielded their fruits, every one of which hath been sent down in the form of a Prophet, bearing a Message to God’s creatures in each of the worlds whose number God, alone, in His all-encompassing Knowledge, can reckon.

order.why: Face the urgency of peace in a world at war.
shortened: Consider His Holiness Baha'u'llah and his teaching. They are the spirit of this cycle - the light of this age. They illumine the dark places of humanity, for they address themselves to the heart of the race. For instance, the greatest evil of this century is war. In the new age Baha'u'llah has prohibited war. The need of this century is universal peace - Baha'u'llah has instituted it.

order.why: Read peace as a subject of sustained public address.
Explore unity through the image of one shepherd.
shortened: The differences of the various religions are the results of dogmas and imitations, so we must give up dogmas and turn our faces to the foundation of religion. Dogmas have always been the cause of strife, while religion was always the cause of Unity. Baha'u'llah proclaimed that religion will again bring love and friendship to mankind; if it does not fulfill this duty, then is it a failure.

order.why: Consider the reported claim about the spirit of the time.
shortened: Consider His Holiness Baha Ollah and His teachings. They are the spirit of this cycle, the light of this century, and they illumine the dark corners of humanity. Whosoever has heard them has confessed that these teachings are in accord with the spirit of this period.

order.why: Read the historical rhetoric within its supplied setting.
Consider an influence whose source may go unrecognized.
shortened: All the peoples of the earth are astir in this age, yet have failed to discover the reason and cause thereof.

order.why: Close with the bird of love as an image of renewed life.
shortened: Know thou that My teachings are pure love for all creatures and infinite grace for every human being. O handmaid of God! Thou shalt see with the eyes of joy that the bird of the love of God has spread its wings on all horizons as a result of the teachings of Bahaiuillah, because they are the spirit of the world of being in the body of mankind, and the light that is shining upon the horizons of creation.

order.why: Ask how scientific change relates to renewed religious teaching.
Open with the possibility of practicing teachings before adopting a name.

questions: What would count as evidence that a spiritual teaching is meeting the needs of an age?
How can openness to change be distinguished from uncritical admiration of novelty?
What might people contribute to a shared transformation even when they understand its source differently?
How do the passages connect inward renewal with practical advances in peace, knowledge, and justice?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the contribution of every person and group to a shared social future.
Explore the relation between inner transformation and changed outward conditions.

references.label: 1 · Luke 12:54–57 — discerning the time
references.note: Jesus contrasts skill in predicting weather with difficulty in recognizing the significance of the present time, then asks his hearers to judge what is right. Read that challenge alongside the compilation’s accounts of a new age. What forms of attention, judgment, and action would genuine discernment require?

subjects.introduction: The old alchemists searched for a substance that could turn base metal into gold. Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá take up that dream and give it to the soul. Touched by the divine Elixir, a dull heart becomes tender, black stone becomes diamond, an insignificant plant grows into a blessed tree, and timid, doubting people find themselves calm, certain and brave. Bahá’u’lláh sets a demanding measure on this hope: a Revelation that left human character unchanged would prove its own futility, for true transformation must show both in the inner life and in outward conditions. Augustine’s long struggle, ended in a single moment by a sentence of Paul [1], reminds us how suddenly such a change can come. Yet love, a timely word and service to an ailing world are also named as the means through which the Elixir works, day after day. To follow this thread is to enter the mystery of the second birth, of faith attained in the twinkling of an eye, and of the spirit of faith that remakes a person in the likeness of God.
subjects.arc: Begin with tenderness and the making of a jewel, test transformation through its effects, and explore both sudden and continuing change.

order.why: Explains spiritual alchemy through love and knowledge transforming human souls into pure gold.
Open with transformation made recognizable in a tender heart. Read the fuller supplied account of a responsive heart.
shortened: So without the intermediary of the Holy Spirit man would remain dull, helpless and deprived of all attainment. But touched by that Divine Elixir he becomes tender, loving, responsive, and capable of every perfection of life.

order.why: Give inward change the vividness of a stone becoming a jewel.
shortened: O loved handmaidens of God! Consider not your present merits and capacities, rather fix your gaze on the favours and confirmations of the Blessed Beauty, because His everlasting grace will make of the insignificant plant a blessed tree, will turn the mirage into cool water and wine; will cause the forsaken atom to become the very essence of being, the puny one erudite in the school of knowledge.
It will transmute the stone into a ruby of great price, and fill the sea shells with brilliant pearls.

order.why: Widen the imagery toward a flourishing garden.
State the test of changed character and outward conditions. Consider a change recognized through a different pattern of conduct. Explore the possibility of a decisive inward turning.
shortened: It is evident that nothing short of this mystic transformation could cause such spirit and behavior, so utterly unlike their previous habits and manners, to be made manifest in the world of being. For their agitation was turned into peace, their doubt into certitude, their timidity into courage. Such is the potency of the Divine Elixir, which, swift as the twinkling of an eye, transmuteth the souls of men!

And yet, is not the object of every Revelation to effect a transformation in the whole character of mankind, a transformation that shall manifest itself, both outwardly and inwardly, that shall affect both its inner life and external conditions? For if the character of mankind be not changed, the futility of God's universal Manifestation would be apparent.

order.why: Connect a spiritual remedy with urgent human needs.
Consider how remembered words may enter a timely conversation.
Hear the elixir image within prayer.
shortened: I beg of Thee, O my God, by Thy most exalted Word which Thou hast ordained as the Divine Elixir unto all who are in Thy realm, the Elixir through whose potency the crude metal of human life hath been transmuted into purest gold, O Thou in Whose hands are both the visible and invisible kingdoms, to ordain that my choice be conformed to Thy choice and my wish to Thy wish, that I may be entirely content with that which Thou didst desire, and be wholly satisfied with what Thou didst destine for me by Thy bounteousness and favor.

order.why: Explore the power attributed to a few transformed people.
shortened: No more than a mere handful, however, hath been found willing to cleave to His Cause, or to become the instruments for its promotion. These few have been endued with the Divine Elixir that can, alone, transmute into purest gold the dross of the world, and have been empowered to administer the infallible remedy for all the ills that afflict the children of men.

order.why: Relate change to the cultivation of divine likeness.
shortened: This is the water that allays every thirst one; this is the Divine Elixir that changes man into the image and likeness of the Almighty.

order.why: Encounter the strongest contrasts used to express transformation.
Return to love as an agent of change.
Hear the assurance that an entire character can change.
End with a scholar’s interpretation of the elixir’s symbolism.

questions: What changes in conduct would make the metaphor of spiritual transformation credible?
How might a sudden awakening and a gradual change of habit support one another?
What is the relationship between a changed heart and changed outward conditions in these passages?
How could a word, an act of love, or a response to need become a turning point for someone?

neighbors.invitation: Explore how teachings are described as releasing latent human possibilities.
Consider transformation on the scale of conflict giving way to peace.

references.label: 1 · Augustine, Confessions VIII.12 — a turning through reading
references.note: Augustine describes prolonged inward conflict followed by a decisive response to a passage from Paul. Compare this particular account of conversion with the compilation’s language of rapid spiritual change. What comes before the turning point, and what changed commitments make its significance visible afterward?

subjects.introduction: Human speech arrives one syllable after another and dies away as it is spoken. Bahá’u’lláh describes a Word of God that appeared without syllable or sound and is sanctified from every property and substance, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that in the world of God there is no past, present or future: yesterday and tomorrow are reckonings made from the earth, unknown in the sun. To think this through is to learn a distinction between kinds of beginning, between what depends on God in time and what depends on God in essence, so that eternity ceases to mean merely an endless length of days. The reality of Christ, the Word, did not begin at his baptism in the Jordan. Augustine’s meditation on an eternal utterance, and his question why there could be no time before time, offer a kindred attempt to say the same thing [1]. The inquiry leads on to the Word of God as the cause of creation, to the preexistence of the Manifestation of God, to the mystery of emanation, and to how a timeless source can still speak to the needs of one particular hour.
subjects.arc: Start beyond syllables and sequence, distinguish different kinds of beginning, and explore how a timeless source is encountered within history.

order.why: Open with a Word that exceeds ordinary properties of speech.
Consider the spiritual realm beyond temporal sequence.
shortened: In the world of God there is no past, present, or future: All of these are one. So when Christ said, "In the beginning was the Word," He meant that it was, is, and shall be; for in the world of God there is no time.

order.why: Explicitly states that a divine word is not bounded by temporal limitations and radiates through all worlds and times.
Distinguish historical events from the origin of prophetic reality.
shortened: Now, the reality of prophethood, which is the Word of God and the state of perfect divine manifestation, has neither beginning nor end, but its radiance varies like that of the sun.

In the Gospel it is said: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God." It follows then that Christ did not attain His Messianic station and His perfections at the moment of His baptism, when the Holy Spirit descended upon Him in the form of a dove. Rather, the Word of God has always been, and will ever remain, in the loftiest heights of sanctity.

order.why: Introduce temporal and essential senses of preexistence. Return to the distinction between kinds of beginning.
Read the reported relativity of time through its analogy.
shortened: And likewise He says that in the spiritual world and divine Kingdom there is no time and place, since times and limits are relative matters, like east and west, south and north, night and day, month and year - these all are relative to the earth, not the celestial sun.

order.why: Connect a present utterance with the voice at Sinai.
shortened: And that Word is an utterance that has appeared and risen from the dawning-place of the Kingdom of exposition and flows and courses from the mouth of the Divine Will. That which is revealed today from the direction of the Throne has been that Divine Word, and this is that same Word which the Interlocutor heard at Sinai and thereby gained victory.

order.why: Consider what endures when other things pass away.
Distinguish divine knowledge from a cause operating in temporal order.
shortened: Question: When an action which someone will perform becomes the object of God's knowledge and is recorded in the "Guarded Tablet" of destiny, is it possible to resist it?

Answer: The knowledge of a thing is not the cause of its occurrence; for the essential knowledge of God encompasses the realities of all things both before and after they come to exist, but it is not the cause of their existence.
Rather, that knowledge is freed from the distinctions of past, present and future, and is identical with the realization of all things without being the cause of that realization.

order.why: Examine essential dependence without a temporal beginning.
shortened: The first thing to emanate from God is that universal reality which the ancient philosophers termed the "First Intellect" and which the people of Baha call the "Primal Will." This emanation, with respect to its action in the world of God, is not limited by either time or place and has neither beginning nor end, for in relation to God the beginning and the end are one and the same. The pre-existence of God is both essential and temporal, while the origination of the contingent world is essential but not temporal, as we have already explained another day at table.

order.why: Return to the eternity attributed to the divine essence.
End with the reported image of an eternal present.
Hear the opening of John’s Gospel already present in the source.
Consider a reported explanation of priority and honor.
Explore first and last in another reported conversation.
Read Augustine’s account of an eternal utterance.
Follow his question about time itself having a beginning.

questions: How does eternity understood as beyond sequence differ from time that simply never ends?
What do the passages distinguish when they speak of temporal and essential dependence?
