How might a timeless source address the needs of a particular historical moment?
Where do analogies drawn from speech, light, and human memory clarify the subject, and where do they reach their limits?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the relation between the Manifestation and the radiance of the Spirit.
Consider a word’s power to impart new life within a changing age.

references.label: 1 · Augustine, Confessions XI.7 and XI.13 — utterance and time
references.note: Augustine contrasts sequential human speech with an eternal divine utterance and asks why there could be no earlier time before time existed. The compilation already includes excerpts from this discussion. Read their fuller setting beside the Bahá’í distinctions between temporal priority, essential dependence, and the historical appearance of a Manifestation.

subjects.introduction: When Táhirih entered a room, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recalled, even the learned fell silent. A clergyman’s daughter who loved knowledge, she read of the Báb’s mission and believed at once, received her name from Him; thereafter neither husband, family, prison nor the Sháh’s decree could still her voice. In the governor’s house, during a wedding, the guests abandoned the bride to gather round her. On the plain of Badasht she lifted her veil and asked whether what God had created pure she should call impure. Her courage sits beside a quieter theme: the Báb’s insistence that she was innocent of the charges made against her, that no believer should deny or harm her, and that disputes about her station be met with silence rather than judgment. She called the day of her death her wedding day. Paul’s declaration that in Christ there is neither male nor female offers one way to ask what spiritual equality demands of social life [1]. Her story opens outward into the Letters of the Living, the figure of Quddús, and the conference of Badasht that announced a new day.
subjects.arc: Encounter Táhirih through learning and speech, place courage beside protection, and consider the lasting influence attributed to her life.

order.why: Open with learning and courage under pressure.
Consider the distinction accorded to this remarkable woman.
Connect freedom from worldly concern with a public spiritual vocation.
Follow the remembered power of speech within confinement.
Explore the connection made with women’s freedom.
shortened: Amongst the women of our own time is Qurratu'l-'Ayn, the daughter of a Muhammadan priest. At the time of the appearance of the Bab she showed such tremendous courage and power that all who heard her were astonished. She threw aside her veil despite the immemorial custom of the women of Persia, and although it was considered impolite to speak with men, this heroic woman carried on controversies with the most learned men, and in every meeting she vanquished them. The Persian Government took her prisoner; she was stoned in the streets, anathematized, exiled from town to town, threatened with death, but she never failed in her determination to work for the freedom of her sisters.

order.why: Bring the Báb’s instruction to protect her into view.
Read further counsel against causing harm amid disagreement.
shortened: As for what you asked about people's differences regarding Tahirih, the essence of what should be accepted about her is that it is incumbent upon all to remain silent concerning her station, and that she was a leaf who believed in her Lord.
When she advanced in the knowledge of the family of God, it is not befitting for a believer to deny her or harm her. She did not rule except by what was detailed in the Book.

order.why: Consider a reported intervention concerning her captivity.
shortened: We immediately summoned Muhammad-Hadiy-i-Farhadi, and gave him the necessary directions to release her from her captivity, and escort her to the capital. As the enemy had seized Our house, We were unable to accommodate her indefinitely in Our home. Accordingly, We arranged for her transference from Our house to that of the Minister of War, who, in those days, had been disgraced by his sovereign and had been deported to Kashan. We requested his sister, who still was numbered among Our friends, to act as hostess to Tahirih.

order.why: Encounter the restraint of violence in a reported conflict.
shortened: None of our companions had remained in Niyala except Tahirih and a young man from Shiraz, Mirza 'Abdullah. The violence with which we were assailed had brought desolation into our camp. I found no one into whose custody I could deliver Tahirih except that young man, who displayed on that occasion a courage and determination that were truly surprising. Sword in hand, undaunted by the savage assault of the inhabitants of the village, who had rushed to plunder our property, he sprang forward to stay the hand of the assailants. Though himself wounded in several parts of his body, he risked his life to protect our property. I bade him desist from his act. When the tumult had subsided, I approached a number of the inhabitants of the village and was able to convince them of the cruelty and shamefulness of their behaviour.

order.why: Read the recollection of Badasht in its supplied form.
shortened: Qurratu'l-'Ayn was a Persian woman without fame and importance -- unknown, like all other Persian women. When she saw Baha'u'llah, she changed completely, visibly, and looked within another world.

She became so attracted to the divine threshold that she forsook everything and went forth to the plain of Badasht, no fear in her heart, dauntless, intrepid, openly proclaiming the message of light which had come to her. The Persian government stood against her. They made every effort to quiet her, they imprisoned her in the governor's house, but she continued to speak. Then she was taken and killed.

order.why: Recounts Tahirih’s appearance at Badasht and the proclamation that produced upheaval among those present.
Consider language of spiritual station that requires close interpretation.
shortened: For many have made claims of divinity and lordship - His Holiness Quddus, may my spirit be sacrificed for him, revealed a book on the interpretation of Samad where from beginning to end it is "I am God", and the honorable Tahirih raised "I am God" to the highest heavens in Badasht, and likewise some loved ones in Badasht, and the Blessed Beauty in the Qasidiy-i-Varqa'iyyih states: "All divinities became divine from a sprinkling of my command, and all lords became lordly from an overflow of my wisdom."

order.why: Retain a reported recollection without turning it into a settled chronology.
shortened: After being released, she went with a number of believers to a celebration outside the city, in a grove near a deserted village. The Blessed Perfection was present. It was a meeting filled with faith, love, and rejoicing. In speaking to the meeting, she became so inspired she removed the cover from her face. Her mother and some of her relatives were present, and her action produced a great commotion among them. When the news came to the ears of the Muhammadans, their charges and persecutions against her became violent and bitter. Finally, she was taken away from her friends and put to death. She died a martyr and a heroine. In her impassioned speech she had said, ' What God has created pure shall I call impure?' removing her veil as she said it.

order.why: Hear the narrative of confinement and her final days.
shortened: She was imprisoned in the governor's house where, by chance, a wedding was being celebrated with all manner of festivity, music, song, food and drink. But Qurratu'l-'Ayn spoke with such power that all abandoned the wedding festivities and gathered around her. No one paid attention to the wedding while she alone spoke. Though the Shah had ordered her execution, and although she had never adorned herself in her lifetime, on that day she adorned herself, which astonished everyone. When asked why, she replied, "This is my wedding day." With perfect dignity and composure she went to that garden. While all were saying she would be killed, she continued to proclaim, "I am that trumpet-call mentioned in the Gospel!" In this state, they martyred her in the garden and cast her into a well.

order.why: Consider the influence attributed to her example.
shortened: That one who first awoke them, who gave her life for this noble cause, was Qurratu'l'Ain. Blessed is she among women!"

order.why: Complicate a simplified picture of unveiling through another report.
Return to the Báb’s affirmation of her understanding.
shortened: And as to attributing such matters unto the Pure Leaf: verily do I call God to witness that she is free and innocent of all this, and hath believed in naught save that which is set forth in the clear Book.

Wherefore should he who hath followed Me repudiate her? For she speaketh not save through the shining guides from among the People of Infallibility and the radiant tokens from among the people of truth.

order.why: Hear recognition of her poetry.
Read the bridal imagery used in remembrance of her death.
shortened: Kurat-el-Ayn had attained to this supreme state.

Although she never cared for dress, that day she wore her best white silk dress and jewelry and perfumed herself with the most fragrant attar of roses. She hailed the chamber of death as a happy bride entering the nuptial bower of the bridegroom.

questions: How do learning, eloquence, and spiritual conviction reinforce one another in these portraits?
What responsibilities arise for a community when a person’s voice challenges familiar boundaries?
How should the different kinds of testimony here shape the questions we ask about Táhirih’s life?
What measures of a life’s influence emerge from the contrast between public power and enduring spiritual example?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the practical challenge of making room for people of every background.
Explore the demand that the protection one seeks for oneself extend to women.

references.label: 1 · Galatians 3:26–29 — unity across inherited divisions
references.note: Paul’s account of belonging to Christ places male and female, slave and free, and Jew and Greek within a shared religious identity. Compare that affirmation with the questions of voice and recognition raised by Táhirih’s portrayal. What further work is involved in translating spiritual equality into social relationships and opportunities?

subjects.displayTitle: John the Baptist: preparing the way
subjects.introduction: John fasted in the wilderness and was said to have a devil; Jesus ate and drank with His companions and was called a glutton. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá points to that pair of objections because it shows how refusal can outlive its own reasons. John’s vocation was entirely directed toward another’s coming: he called a wounded people to repentance, washed them as a sign of hearts made ready, felt the Holy Spirit in Christ when the dove descended as a metaphor, and lost his head for it. His own Gospel account of denying that he was Elijah while bearing witness to the One who came after him is worth reading alongside [1], for the Bahá’í writings resolve the apparent contradiction by distinguishing the lamp from the light: John was not the man Elijah, but the same light shone through him. Bahá’u’lláh then draws the parallel closer to home, likening John’s relation to Christ to that of the Báb, the Primal Point, to His own Revelation. From here the way leads toward Christ and the beginnings of Christianity, and toward the station and claims of the Báb.
subjects.arc: Begin with contradictory objections, explore preparation and purification, and approach spiritual return through the distinction between a lamp and its light.

order.why: Connect preparation with the hope offered by a physician.
Open with opposite habits provoking the same refusal to recognize.
shortened: They said to the Son of Mary that John the Baptist fasted and clung to asceticism and piety, while He and His companions ate and drank. The Spirit said: "John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say he hath a devil. The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, behold a gluttonous man." To those of insight it is clear that by John is meant John the Baptist, and by Son of Man the Son of Mary.

order.why: Introduce John’s work of preparing the path.
Place his witness within the prophetic story.
Consider baptism in relation to repentance.
Explore purification of the heart as its spiritual meaning.
shortened: Baptism by John the Baptist was only a symbol used to signify that the hearts had been purified by repentance (they were grown people, not children).

order.why: Ask what the image of the descending dove signifies.
shortened: The story about the dove is simply a metaphor. No dove came down. Amongst the people, John the Baptist felt that the Holy Spirit was in Christ. The Holy Spirit was always with Christ.

order.why: Hear the denial of a literal identity with Elijah.
Set beside it the scriptural affirmation of return.
Consider the apparent contradiction through spiritual unity.
Distinguish physical identity from a returning spiritual quality.
Clearly distinguishes John’s spiritual return as Elijah from return of the same individual soul.
Retain another reported discussion of the same difficulty.
shortened: Then, again, He says that John the Baptist was the Elijah foretold, who would come before Christ. This is also an explicit text of the Gospel, whereas when they asked of John the Baptist, 'Art thou Elias?' he said, 'I am not.' Christ said he was Elijah. The disciples declared that this John the Baptist was the prophet prophesied, whereas when they asked of him he said he was not. Now, he was either Elijah, or he was not! What is your view of it? How can it be interpreted?"
The man was dumbfounded.

order.why: Read the reported account of John’s life in its own setting.
Consider witness from within imprisonment.
shortened: He is the true Herald Who appeared to inform the people, that they might make themselves ready and clear the paths, even as John son of Zacharias, who is mentioned in the Books as John the Baptist, gave glad tidings of the appearance of Christ while he was in prison when Jesus son of Mary declared His Cause.

order.why: Reflect on the cost associated with his vocation.
shortened: And if you seek the flame of Sinai and the gleam of light, hasten with your soul to the wilderness of Sinai. And if you seek the station of John (the Baptist), sacrifice your head and life. And if you wish to inhale the fragrances of the Prince of Martyrs, spill your blood in the plain of tribulation and ordeal. This is the station of the lovers and this is the description of the yearning ones.

order.why: Place the remembered death within a wider meditation on persecution.
shortened: O My handmaiden, ponder upon the son of Zachariah, whose blessed head was severed for the sake of a harlot, and the head of Husayn which was raised upon a spear at the command of a transgressor, and the Temple of the Bayan which was suspended in the air. Had the world any worth, the gems of existence would never have been afflicted with such tribulations.

order.why: Follow qualities recurring across prophetic lives.
Consider the analogy of dawn and a herald.
Explore the comparison between John and the Báb.
shortened: Consider somewhat the Bayan: The example of this Revelation and the Revelation of the Point of the Bayan is exactly like the appearance of the son of Zachariah and Jesus the son of Mary. The son of Zachariah, despite his station of prophethood and the greatness of his rank, gave the people glad tidings of the appearance of the Spirit, and both were in the same age.

order.why: Close with different lamps bearing a common light.
shortened: And this Spirit hath both restitution and return, inasmuch as it consists of the Light of God and the unconditioned Grace. So, having regard to this state and station, Christ announced that John the Baptist was Elias, who was to come before Christ (Matt. 11:14). And the likeness of this station is as that of lamps kindled (from one another): for these in respect to their glasses and oil-holders, are different, but in respect to their light, One, and in respect to their illumination, One; nay, each one is identical with the other, without imputation of plurality, or diversity or multiplicity or separateness.

questions: How does the opening contrast expose the ways expectations can prevent recognition?
What might it mean to prepare others for a truth or opportunity that will lead them beyond one’s own role?
How do the passages reconcile John’s denial that he is Elijah with the claim of Elijah’s return?
What becomes clearer when baptism and the dove are read for their spiritual meanings, and what questions still require attention to the narratives?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the different kinds of prophetic role distinguished in the compilation.
Consider the language used for a person who prepares the way for a Manifestation.

references.label: 1 · John 1:19–34 — denial, preparation, and witness
references.note: The Gospel places John’s denial of being the Christ or Elijah beside his account of preparing the way and witnessing the Spirit descend. Read these details alongside the compilation’s treatment of spiritual return and baptism. What does each interpretation take identity, recognition, and testimony to involve?

subjects.introduction: A polished mirror held up to the sun shows the sun entire, yet the sun never leaves the sky. That is how ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains the Perfect Man: the one reality in which the full splendour of the divine attributes appears, so that to know the Manifestation of God is to know God, since the Essence itself can never be known. Every created thing receives a ray; this one receives the whole, and the ancient and the contingent remain forever distinct. Colossians calls Christ the image of the invisible God, in whom all fullness dwells [1], a claim with its own theological grammar that rewards careful comparison. The phrase has other homes too, in the Qur’án’s account of the Spirit appearing to Mary, in Bahá’u’lláh’s word for the herald who prepares souls before each new Revelation, and in the soul’s own growth, which advances in perfections though not in station. An exemplary life enlarges those who meet it rather than merely drawing their admiration. The path leads on to the station of the Manifestation of God, to sinlessness and infallibility, and to the human being as the fruit of creation.
subjects.arc: Begin with the mirror, explore the distinctive station of a Manifestation, and then examine the phrase’s other uses without flattening their differences.

order.why: Relate the complete expression of thought to the Word.
shortened: Man is the sum of Creation, and the Perfect Man is the expression of the complete thought of the Creator -- the Word of God.

order.why: Open with perfection pictured as a polished mirror.
shortened: The Perfect Man is as a polished mirror reflecting the Sun of Truth, manifesting the attributes of God.

order.why: Explain the Manifestation’s relation to divine attributes and essence.
shortened: For the other beings have each received only a portion of that light, but the universal Manifestation of God is the mirror held before this Sun, and the latter manifests itself therein with all its perfections, attributes, signs and effects.

The knowledge of the reality of the Divinity is in no wise possible, but the knowledge of the Manifestations of God is the knowledge of God, for the bounties, splendours and attributes of God are manifest in them. Thus, whoso attains to the knowledge of the Manifestations of God attains to the knowledge of God, and whoso remains heedless of them remains bereft of that knowledge.

order.why: Consider the distinctive individual described by the text.
Place human perfection within a wider account of creation.
Examine the claim concerning the enduring presence of perfection.
Ask how one perfected life bears fruit in others.
Encounter the Báb’s language of self-effacement and truth.
Read the phrase within the account of Mary and the Spirit.
shortened: In the Qur'an it is said: "And We sent Our Spirit to her, and He took before her the form of a perfect man", meaning that the Holy Spirit assumed a human form, as an image appears in a mirror, and conversed with Mary.

order.why: Distinguish growth in perfections from a change of station.
shortened: Both before and after casting off this elemental frame, the human soul progresses in perfections but not in station. The progression of all created things culminates in perfect man, and no greater being than him exists: Man, having reached the human station, can progress only in perfections and not in station, for there is no higher station to which he can find passage than that of a perfect man.

order.why: Describes the Perfect Manifestation as the intermediary gathering divine and created stations.
Return to the mirror without imagining the sun descending into it.
shortened: Thus, among created beings, man is the most perfect of creatures. By man is meant the perfect individual, and that perfect individual is like a mirror wherein divine perfections appear and are visible. However, the Sun does not descend from its height of sanctity and enter into the mirror, but when the mirror is pure and faces the Sun of Reality, the perfections of the Sun of Reality - which are its rays and heat - become manifest and visible in that mirror. These souls are the Holy Manifestations of God.

order.why: Explains the Perfect Man through the mirror analogy while rejecting incarnation or transformation of the divine essence.
Close with the phrase applied to preparation for a new revelation.
shortened: The sign of the invisible heaven must needs be revealed in the person of that perfect man who, before each Manifestation appeareth, educateth, and prepareth the souls of men for the advent of the divine Luminary, the Light of the unity of God amongst men.

order.why: Hear the prophetic mirror image in a further account.

questions: What does the mirror image affirm about the Manifestation, and what does it rule out?
How does the meaning of “perfect man” change across the passages collected here?
What is the difference between developing a perfection and claiming a particular spiritual station?
How might an exemplary life enlarge the capacities of other people rather than merely attract admiration?

neighbors.invitation: Consider why the terms prophet and Manifestation are not simply interchangeable.
Explore the relationship between a divine source and its spiritual radiance.

references.label: 1 · Colossians 1:15–20 — the image of the invisible God
references.note: Colossians relates Christ to the invisible God, creation, fullness, and reconciliation through the cross. Compare its account with the compilation’s language of a perfect mirror of divine attributes. Attend to the distinct theological claims: the comparison opens questions about revelation through a person without making the accounts identical.

subjects.introduction: Every Manifestation of God is a prophet, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá said, but not every prophet is a Manifestation. The word carries more than one kind of work. Some prophets are independent: each founds a religion, reveals a Book, and clothes the world in a new attire, shining with an essential light like the sun. Others are followers and promulgators, recipients of hidden inspiration who uphold a teaching already given, and some are prophets whose sphere is limited to a single place or country, like Isaiah beside Jesus. Bahá’u’lláh describes the many ways a message is received: through a Book and clear proof, through inspired speech, through angelic messengers, through the Spirit speaking within the breast. The Qur’an too speaks of messengers raised in degrees above one another [1]. Such distinctions are not a ranking of worth but a way of honouring each vocation: who brings a new law, who prepares a people, who renews their response. They lead onward into the differences among the Manifestations themselves and into the twofold and threefold station in which divinity and humanity meet.
subjects.arc: Clarify the central distinction, explore different scopes and modes of prophetic work, and return to the fuller explanations behind the categories.

order.why: Complicate a simple binary with a threefold account. Close with the separately supplied summary of three kinds.
shortened: Answer: There are three kinds of divine Prophets. One kind are the universal Manifestations, which are even as the sun.

Another kind of Prophets are followers and promulgators, not leaders and law-givers, but they are nonetheless the recipients of the hidden inspirations of God. Yet another kind are Prophets Whose prophethood has been limited to a particular locality. But the universal Manifestations are all-encompassing: They are like the root, and all others are as the branches; they are like the sun, and all others are as the moon and the stars.

order.why: Begin with the concise distinction between prophet and Manifestation.
shortened: Master:	"Yes and no, namely: each Manifestation has His prophetic mission and His prophetic character, but not each Prophet is at the same time a Manifestation. This, my friends, will immediately be shown, when we look at some of the Prophets and Manifestations separately.

order.why: Distinguishes a universal Manifestation inaugurating a cycle from later Manifestations arising under that cycle's shadow.
Distinguishes dependent ranks, the Prophets of Israel, and independent Manifestations of universal divine authority.
Introduce independent and dependent prophetic roles. Return to the fuller account of new dispensations and their supporters.
shortened: Answer: Prophets are in general of two kinds. Some are independent Prophets Who are followed, while others are not independent and are themselves followers.

The independent Prophets are each the Author of a divine religion and the Founder of a new Dispensation. At their advent the world is clothed in a new attire, a new religion is established and a new Book revealed.

order.why: Consider differing modes of receiving and conveying a message.
Make the distinction concrete through named examples.
Explore the scope of a teacher’s influence.
shortened: In the case of Prophets, some have the power to sway and subdue one country only, such as Syria, some have the power to sway many more countries.

order.why: Set spiritual instructors beside other kinds of thinkers.
shortened: Teachers are of two kinds: universal and special. The universal Instructors are the Prophets of God, and the special teachers are the philosophers. The philosophers are capable of educating and training a limited circle of human souls, whereas the holy, divine Manifestations of God confer general education upon humanity.

order.why: Read a reported explanation of the word’s differing uses.

questions: What becomes clearer when prophetic figures are distinguished by vocation or scope rather than placed under a single label?
How do the roles of inaugurating, preparing, and renewing a religious community support one another?
What might be lost if these categories were used without attending to each tradition’s own language and understanding?

neighbors.invitation: Explore a comparison between two figures who prepare the way for another.
Consider the distinctive relationship between a Manifestation and divine attributes.

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 2:253 — differing gifts among messengers
references.note: The verse speaks of differing degrees among messengers and names the gifts given to Jesus, while also recalling later conflict among followers. Compare this recognition of difference with the compilation’s distinctions among prophetic roles. The verse does not itself reproduce the same categories; consider both what the comparison clarifies and where it leaves questions open.

subjects.introduction: Once in every month, Bahá’u’lláh commands, offer a feast, though only water be served, for God’s purpose is to bind hearts together. The whole institution grows from that sentence. Tea alone will do, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds; what matters is that the friends gather in love, turn their faces to the Kingdom, speak of the teachings and leave spiritually restored, endued with a power not of this world. He wants them to empty their hearts of everything but God before they walk in, and the Báb’s rhythm of nineteen days makes the renewal a habit rather than an event. Devotion, consultation and simple friendship are meant to deepen one another at one table, and preparing the programme, the room and the welcome is itself a service. Paul’s rebuke of a Corinthian meal at which the poor were shamed while others feasted asks the question any such gathering must face: how does it treat the people actually present [1]? From here the path leads toward spiritual and devotional gatherings, toward the fellowship of the friends, and toward the Holy Days of the Bahá’í calendar.
subjects.arc: Begin with the simplest hospitality, explore the gathering’s spiritual purpose, and bring its devotional, consultative, and social dimensions together.

order.why: Open with water alone as a sufficient offering of hospitality.
Connect hosting with means rather than display.
Reinforce simplicity through bread and water.
shortened: If possible have a general meeting every nineteen days even though it be to partake of only water and bread.

order.why: Introduce the recurring rhythm of nineteen days.
Encourages the recurring nineteen-day feast as a means of unity and attracting divine confirmation.
Ask what the gathering should accomplish for its participants.
shortened: Whatsoever gathering is arranged with the utmost love, and where those who attend are turning their faces toward the Kingdom of God, and where the discourse is of the Teachings of God, and the effect of which is to cause those present to advance -- that gathering is the Lord's, and that festive table hath come down from heaven.
It is my hope that this feast will be given on one day out of every nineteen, for it bringeth you closer together; it is the very well-spring of unity and loving-kindness.

order.why: Picture the friends as leaves in a shared life.
shortened: It is the Nineteen Day Feast. A group of faithful friends and radiant leaves are gathered in supplication to the Abha Kingdom. All blessings are present and prepared, and the table is infinitely pleasing.

order.why: Explore material and spiritual nourishment together.
Consider the seriousness of the gathering’s purpose.
Bring prayer into the life of the meeting.
shortened: I beg of God, out of His endless bounties, that many such gatherings will be held, and that the Nineteen Day festivity will also be observed, so that men and women believers will occupy themselves with making mention of God, and praising and glorifying Him, and guiding the people aright.

order.why: Look toward inspiration expressed in service.
shortened: Thou didst write of the Nineteen Day festivity, and this rejoiced my heart. These gatherings cause the divine table to descend from Heaven, and draw down the confirmations of the All-Merciful. My hope is that the breathings of the Holy Spirit will be wafted over them, and that each one present shall, in great assemblies, with an eloquent tongue and a heart flooded with the love of God, set himself to acclaiming the rise of the Sun of Truth, the dawn of the Day-Star that lighteth all the World....

order.why: Read magnificence beside the earlier permission for simplicity.
shortened: Hold the Nineteen Day Feast with utmost glory.

order.why: Consider the heart’s preparation before entering.
Connect fellowship with charitable endeavor.
shortened: This feast is held to foster comradeship and love, to call God to mind and supplicate Him with contrite hearts, and to encourage benevolent pursuits.

order.why: Make hospitality concrete in the host’s own service.
shortened: Let the beloved of God gather together and associate most lovingly and spiritually and happily with one another, conducting themselves with the greatest courtesy and self-restraint. Let them read the holy verses, as well as essays which are of benefit, and the letters of 'Abdu'l-Baha; encourage and inspire one another to love each and all; chant the prayers with serenity and joy; give eloquent talks; and praise the matchless Lord.

order.why: Connect remembrance with deeds and fellowship.
Trace the explanation of its administrative significance.
Read the integrated account of its three dimensions.
shortened: The World Order of Baha'u'llah encompasses all units of human society; integrates the spiritual, administrative and social processes of life; and canalizes human expression in its varied forms towards the construction of a new civilization. The Nineteen Day Feast embraces all these aspects at the very base of society. Functioning in the village, the town, the city, it is an institution of which all the people of Baha are members. It is intended to promote unity, ensure progress, and foster joy....

order.why: Close with fellowship reaching across human distinctions.

questions: What makes hospitality rich when the material offering is simple?
How might devotion, consultation, and friendship deepen one another within the same gathering?
What preparations would help every participant feel both welcome and able to contribute?
What changes in relationships or service might reveal that a Feast has fulfilled its purpose?

neighbors.invitation: Explore a prayer joining unity, forgiveness, and inward composure.
Consider the connection between fellowship and sharing justly.

references.label: 1 · 1 Corinthians 11:20–29 — a meal and the dignity of participants
references.note: Paul rebukes a gathering in which some feast while others go hungry and the poor are shamed. Compare this ethical challenge with the Feast’s permission for simple hospitality and its purpose of unity. The Lord’s Supper has its own sacramental meaning; the comparison concerns how a religious gathering treats the people present.

subjects.introduction: The circle of the righteous has been scattered, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá laments, and the meeting place of the friends destroyed; will God restore them once more? Prayer for a gathering begins in that need rather than in triumph. Those who come bring their shortcomings and ask for forgiveness, composure and the burning away of veils before they ask for anything grander. Then the petitions enlarge the room: let this assembly be a rose garden, a candle shedding light in six directions, a dawning-place of loving-kindness; let these souls be pearls strung on one thread. Psalm 133 gives the same unity the texture of oil running down a beard and dew settling on a mountain [1]. What is sought is never only harmony inside the room. The gathering is to blaze outward, spreading divine fragrances and serving the oneness of humanity, and its sincerity shows in the relationships it helps form. That is the spirit in which spiritual meetings, devotional gatherings and the Feast are held, and these prayers are a doorway into the wider life of prayer itself.
subjects.arc: Begin with reunion after scattering, seek forgiveness and harmony, and follow the prayers toward service beyond the gathering.

order.why: A complete prayer for an assembled group, seeking purification, unity and service to humanity.
Open with the need to gather what has been scattered.
shortened: With every breath I have lifted up my lamentations to the Kingdom of everlasting might, at every step on the path of supplication I have implored God saying: "O Thou kind Lord! The circle of the righteous hath been scattered and the gathering place of the friends hath been destroyed. Wouldst Thou reveal Thy bounties unto them once more? Wouldst Thou shower these friends again with new confirmations that they might come together and become illuminated by the lamp of thy remembrance in their gatherings? O God, the Most Kind! Lift Thy decree that hath disbanded and dispersed these friends! O Compassionate Lord gather this desolate and scattered band.

order.why: Seek love and harmony among those coming together.
shortened: O Lord! These souls have come to this gathering purely out of love and are present with perfect love and harmony.

order.why: Make humility and forgiveness part of that beginning.
Connect unity with composure and the removal of veils.
Consider the harmonizing of purposes around the Word.
shortened: Whenever ye enter the council-chamber, recite this prayer with a heart throbbing with the love of God and a tongue purified from all but His remembrance, that the All-Powerful may graciously aid you to achieve supreme victory:

O God, my God! We are servants of Thine that have turned with devotion to Thy Holy Face, that have detached ourselves from all besides Thee in this glorious Day. We have gathered in this Spiritual Assembly, united in our views and thoughts, with our purposes harmonized to exalt Thy Word amidst mankind.

order.why: Deepen the aspiration toward a common aim.
shortened: O my God! O God! We are servants who have sincerely turned our faces unto Thy Grand Face; severed ourselves from all else save thee in this Great Day and are assembled together in this glorious meeting of one accord and desire, and unanimous in thought to promulgate Thy Word amid Thy creatures.

order.why: Hear the prayer of those drawn together.
shortened: My God, my God! These are servants who have turned toward the right hand of Thy favor, who have gathered together and been attracted by Thy call, and who have acknowledged Thy oneness.

order.why: Let the room open imaginatively into a garden.
shortened: O Pure God! Make this gathering a light to the world, and make this assembly a rose garden and flower bed. Make its meeting place a garden of paradise and its dawning place the dawning-place of the lights of the All-Merciful.

order.why: Attend to the dispositions that make such a garden possible. Read the fuller prayer associated with the earlier garden image.
Turn its inward life toward light in every direction.
shortened: A. A.

O Lord! Make this gathering even as an ignited candle that sheddeth its light to the six directions and illumine and chase away this obscure darkness with the light of Thy revelation. O Lord! Make this assembly a centre of perfections. O Merciful! Make this gathering a dawning-place of Thy loving-kindness.

order.why: Connect the gathering with wider human oneness.
shortened: O Thou compassionate Lord! This Assembly has been organized for the exaltation of God - the Holy Spirit. Assist, confirm it and reinforce it by Thy Heavenly Power so that it may blaze like unto a brilliant flame and may diffuse Merciful Light. That it may illumine the surrounding regions, may promulgate Heavenly Teachings and serve the Oneness of the world of mankind.

order.why: Explore the spreading of spiritual influence.
Ask for assistance in practical affairs.
Imagine unity as the foundation of a shared work.
shortened: O Lord! Adorn their gathering with the lights of Thy unity, illuminate their assembly with the lamp of Thy sanctity, purify their court with the cloud of Thy transcendence, strengthen their foundations with Thy power that vanquisheth all things, make firm their structure with Thy might that is manifested throughout all things, gird up their loins and strengthen their backs, make their affairs easy, and make them emblems of Thy remembrance, wellsprings of Thy praise, torches of Thy love, dawning-places of Thy grace, recipients of Thy inspiration, daysprings of Thy knowledge, and manifestations of Thy signs.

order.why: Keep expectation open to gifts not yet visible.
Encounter the energetic images of light and fire.
Hear joy expressed through faces and chanting.
Seek protection for the assembly.
Close with humility becoming service to others.
shortened: O God! O God! From the unseen kingdom of Thy oneness behold us assembled in this spiritual meeting, believing in Thee, confident in Thy signs, firm in Thy Covenant and Testament, attracted to Thee, set aglow with the fire of Thy love and sincere in Thy Cause. We are servants in Thy vineyard, spreaders of Thy religion, devoted worshipers of Thy countenance, humble towards Thy loved ones, submissive before Thy door, and imploring Thee to confirm us in serving Thy chosen ones, to support us with Thine unseen hosts, to strengthen our loins in Thy servitude and to make us submissive and adoring subjects communing with Thee.

questions: What needs or experiences might people bring into a gathering before they are ready to share a common purpose?
How could the prayers for forgiveness and composure change the quality of a difficult conversation?
What do the images of a garden, necklace, and ocean suggest about unity among distinct persons?
How might a gathering’s prayer become visible in its service to people beyond the room?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the integration of devotion, consultation, and social fellowship.
Consider lovingkindness and equity in relationships with everyone.

references.label: 1 · Psalm 133 — unity pictured as oil and dew
references.note: The psalm celebrates dwelling together through images of anointing oil and life-giving dew. Compare its sensory language with the gardens, pearls, and lamps in these prayers. What can an image communicate about shared life that a general instruction to be united may leave unsaid?

subjects.introduction: A bird has flown from the nests of its homeland, its wings grown weary, until it alights in a verdant garden: this is how ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes a pilgrim arriving. The prayers for pilgrimage know the whole road, the plains and mountains crossed, the seas, the heat and cold, the need for protection, and they know also the ache of those who left home longing to arrive and were prevented by the hands of others. One supplication does not even know whether arrival has been decreed, and asks only to be accepted either way. Psalm 84 sings the same longing, with sparrows nesting near the altar and pilgrims gaining strength as they go [1]. What is asked for at the threshold is not only a merciful glance but prosperity in one’s affairs, forgiveness for oneself and those represented by the journey, steadfastness afterwards, and deeds that carry the visit into ordinary life. So the pilgrim’s prayer opens onto pilgrimage itself, the law that ordains it and the permission that governs a visit, and onto the wider life of prayer that makes any arrival an inward one.
subjects.arc: Begin with the weary traveler’s longing, acknowledge both arrival and its obstacles, and end with the life and deeds that follow the visit.

order.why: Acknowledge the difficult terrain of the journey.
shortened: O my God, my God! Thou seest Thy sincere servants in religion and Thy near ones who are attracted to the manifest Light. They have traversed plains, heights and valleys, crossed rivers, deserts and mountains, plunging through the depths of seas to reach the Spot of Light, the Dawning-place of signs, the Center of mysteries, the circumambulating place of the righteous and the kissing place of the free, enkindled with the fire of Thy love, their hearts throbbing with love for Thy Oneness.

order.why: Open with a weary bird finding the possibility of rest.
shortened: My God, my God! This is a bird that has flown from the nests of its homeland, seeking the flight-realm of the holy birds in the luminous spot. Its wings have grown weary, and its primary and secondary feathers have become exhausted, until it alighted in this verdant garden and was honored to move to these groves and meadows that bring joy to eyes and vision.

order.why: Hear the longing for a sacred place.
Place travel by land and sea within a prayer of trust.
shortened: O my God! O my God! This is Thy servant who hath turned his face toward Thee, hath put his trust in Thee, hath believed in Thee and in Thy most wonderful Verses. Verily he hath traversed seas and countries, making his way to the holy and radiant Land and the fragrant and exalted Threshold, prostrating himself before Thy most exalted Word and drawing nigh unto Thy most lofty Court of mercifulness.

order.why: Attend to the traveler’s need for protection.
Leave room for uncertainty about whether arrival is possible.
shortened: I know not, O my God and my Lord, whether Thou hast ordained for Thy servant to turn toward the lights of Thy countenance, to stand before Thy throne, to stand at Thy gate, and to enter the place which Thou hast made the circling-point of Thy Prophets and Thy Messengers, or whether Thy irrevocable decree hath prevented me from this most great bounty, O Master of nations.

order.why: Include the longing of someone prevented from making the journey.
shortened: These are Thy servants who have left their homes out of longing to meet Thee, and have forsaken their native lands yearning for the court of Thy mighty throne, the visitation of Thy beauty and presence before Thee. They have been prevented therefrom by reason of what the hands of Thy creatures have wrought.

order.why: Connect longing with the acceptance of deeds.
shortened: When thou desirest to turn toward the direction before which all directions have bowed down, say: "O my Lord! I have desired Thy presence and Thy meeting, and to stand before Thy door which hath been opened unto all who are in Thy heaven and on Thine earth.
Accept, then, what I have done and perform in Thy path out of longing for Thy beauty and passionate love for Thee.

order.why: Seek assistance at the threshold of arrival.
shortened: I bear witness, O my God, my Purpose and my Desire, that Thou didst strengthen me and assist me until I traversed land and sea and attained unto Thy gate, which Thou hast opened unto the faces of all who are in Thy earth and Thy heaven.

order.why: Consider the encounter with revealed words.
shortened: O Thou Who rulest over whatsoever Thou willest!

Glory be unto Thee, O my God! Thou seest a servant from among Thy servants who hath left his home, turning towards Thy countenance and drawing nigh unto the ocean of Thy mercy and the heaven of Thy grace, until he attained Thy presence and stood before Thy face and heard Thy verses.

order.why: Ask for a merciful regard.
Carry practical affairs into the prayer.
shortened: O Lord! This servant of Thine has hastened from the furthest lands to Thy fragrant and radiant Threshold, that he might prostrate himself before Thee in worship, O Lord of Lords!

Lord, open the doors before his face, bestow upon him through Thy mercy beyond measure, make his affairs prosper in their beginning and end, forgive him and me and all the loved ones, and make us among those who have inherited the Book and understood the excellence of divine discourse and drunk from the springhead of certitude a cooling draught.

order.why: Join the visit with grace and forgiveness.
shortened: I implore God to illumine this blessed ground with a light radiating from the Kingdom of Abha and to confirm those who make pilgrimages to this holy ground through the grace of His Mercy, supplicating God to pardon and forgive their sins and to admit them into the depths of the sea of His Mercy forever.

order.why: Seek good beyond the immediate moment of pilgrimage.
Prays for protection, renewed pilgrimage to the Sacred House and good in this world and the next.
Connect the visit with steadfastness.
Remember those represented by another person’s journey.
shortened: O my Lord! This is a branch from among the branches of Thy Tree of Divine Unity, and a twig from among the twigs of the Tree of Thy Oneness. He has arisen to represent Thy servant and has visited Thy Sacred House and circled round Thy holy sanctuary, O my Lord, the Mighty, the All-Knowing. O Lord! Ordain for him abundant reward and great bounty in Thy Most Glorious Kingdom and Thy exalted Companion. Verily, Thou art the Generous, the Most High.

order.why: Hear the hope that the pilgrimage will be accepted.
Relate visiting to actions that are pleasing.
shortened: However, We have pardoned him and We beseech God to assist him to visit His House and draw him nigh unto Him and enable him to do that which He loves and is pleased with.

order.why: Turn toward the joy and influence brought home.
Close with the relation between a visit and enduring deeds.

questions: How do the prayers connect a physical place with an inward condition?
What possibilities of nearness remain for someone who cannot make the journey?
How might pilgrimage become an experience shared with people who stay at home?
What changes in conduct or relationships would carry the meaning of a visit into everyday life?

neighbors.invitation: Consider how a prayer for reunion gives voice to people who are scattered.
Explore preparation of the heart as a dwelling for a sacred presence.

references.label: 1 · Psalm 84 — longing, journey, and shelter
references.note: Psalm 84 moves from longing for the sanctuary to the image of birds finding a home and pilgrims gaining strength on their journey. Compare these images with the weary bird and returning traveler in the compilation. What is sought in arrival, and how is a journey’s spiritual meaning carried through difficulty?

subjects.introduction: Work is meant to give a person self-assurance and dignity, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, and then He asks why so many are robbed of both by drudgery. Having seen the coal miners and the ship labourers, He answers concretely: a fair daily wage, a share in the profits of the enterprise, workers who elect their own representatives to consult with the company, and hours short enough to leave leisure to think and grow. He treats fairness as reciprocal, owners bound to kindness and workers to good faith, and insists that a quarrel between them is never merely private, since a nation’s livelihood is one fabric and a tear anywhere is felt everywhere. Deuteronomy’s rule that a poor labourer be paid before the sun sets shows how old and how plain this concern is [1]. The village storehouse, with its graduated tithes and its care for orphans and the infirm, is an example rather than a statute, and the journey it begins leads into justice itself, into the moderation of wealth and poverty, and into a measured reckoning with capitalism and its rivals.
subjects.arc: Start with workers’ dignity and lived conditions, explore shared benefit and public responsibility, and read detailed proposals in light of their explicit limits.

order.why: Open with work as a dignified human activity.
Bring the conditions of miners into view.
Consider hardship in another setting of labor.
Connect shorter hours with the development of human capacities.
shortened: That all mankind might have opportunity, it was necessary to shorten the hours of labor so that the work of the world could be completed without such demand of strain and effort, and all human beings would have leisure to think and develop  individual capacity.

order.why: Widen the aim toward the welfare of all.
Explore a wage combined with participation in profits.
Make fairness a reciprocal responsibility.
Introduce consultation and representation in shared enterprise.
shortened: He was interested in the economic problem and asked the following question: "When the time comes for the working people to become the partners of their employers, will they have their own representatives to consult with the company and will those who invest more capital receive more shares?" Abdul-Baha replied: "Certainly, when the working people become partners with the company, they will select their own representatives for consultation and those who have more capital will earn more money."

order.why: Consider another account of workers as participants.
Place disputes and profit sharing in a concrete reported setting.
Identify the public interest in relations between workers and owners. Read the fuller discussion of mutual rights and public adjudication.
shortened: For instance, the factory owners reap a fortune every day, but the wage the poor workers are paid cannot even meet their daily needs: this is most unfair, and assuredly no just man can accept it. Therefore, laws and regulations should be enacted which would grant the workers both a daily wage and a share in a fourth or fifth of the profits of the factory in accordance with its means, or which would have the workers equitably share in some other way in the profits with the owners.

The intervention of the government and the courts in the problems arising between owners and workers is fully warranted, since these are not such particular matters as are ordinary transactions between two individuals, which do not concern the public and in which the government should have no right to interfere. For problems between owners and workers, though they may appear to be a private matter, are detrimental to the common good, since the commercial, industrial and agricultural affairs, and even the general business of the nation, are all intimately linked together: An impairment to one is a loss to all. And since the problems between owners and workers are detrimental to the common good, the government and the courts have therefore the right to intervene.

order.why: Read the explicit limits on treating examples as fixed laws.
shortened: What hath been stated is only an example and this doth not mean that it should be enforced exactly in this manner. The principle is that as a man's wealth increaseth, his financial obligations should proportionately increase, so that vast riches may not be accumulated in one place. In this manner justice may be exercised between the rich and the poor. Thus there will not be, on one hand, a man owning a thousand million and, on the other, a poor man in need of his necessary subsistence.
These are only the preliminary principles; the House of Justice will arrange and widen them in accordance with time and place.

order.why: Examine the extended proposal for communal revenue and support.
shortened: "The solution begins with the village, and when the village is reconstructed, then the cities will be also. The idea is this, that in each village will be erected a store-house. In the language of Religion it is called the House of Finance. That is a universal store-house, which is commenced in the village. Its administration is through a committee of the wise ones of the community, and with the approval of that committee all the affairs are directed.

"If there is something left over (after these expenditures) it should be given to the Great House of Justice. And thus there will be no want in the village. The people will not remain hungry, they will not remain naked. All will be in the utmost welfare and comfort.

order.why: Advocates voluntary mutual sacrifice and improved conditions instead of antagonism between labor and capital.
Consider a reported institutional arrangement in its historical setting.
shortened: Those villages around the big cities are represented by the House of Justice of that city. The village is the unit. Its wise men are chosen to administer the affairs of the village. For example, there may be a farmer who has no animals, implements or seeds, and this committee will help him. There will be universal banks and the council will borrow money from them and loan it to the people. For instance they will borrow at three per cent and loan to the people at four per cent. The one per cent is for the expenses; and thus the village will have the storehouse.

order.why: Read a reported allocation as a particular proposal.
Return to the bodily costs of difficult labor.
Explore the detailed village storehouse proposal.
shortened: In brief, from among the wise men in every village a board should be set up and the affairs of that village should be under the control of that board. Likewise a general storehouse should be founded with the appointment of a secretary. At the time of the harvest, under the direction of that board, a certain percentage of the entire harvest should be appropriated for the storehouse.

The storehouse has seven revenues: Tithes, taxes on animals, property without an heir, all lost objects found whose owners cannot be traced, one third of all treasure-trove, one third of the produce of all mines, and voluntary contributions.

On the other hand, should a person's income be two hundred, but his needs absolutely essential for his livelihood be five hundred dollars, and provided he hath not been remiss in his work or his farm hath not been blessed with a harvest, such a one must receive help from the general storehouse so that he may not remain in need and may live in comfort.

order.why: Compare the further account of its revenues and uses.
shortened: In every village there must be established a general storehouse which will have a number of revenues. The first revenue will be that of the tenth or tithes. The second revenue [will be derived] from the animals. The third revenue, from the minerals; that is to say, every mine prospected or discovered, a third thereof will go to this vast storehouse. The fourth is this: whosoever dies without leaving any heirs, all his heritage will go to the general storehouse. Fifth, if any treasures shall be found on the land, they should be devoted to this storehouse. All these revenues will be assembled in this storehouse.
In the village no one will remain in need or in want. All will live in the utmost comfort and welfare. Yet no schism will assail the general order of the body politic.

order.why: Close with the distinction between principles and a complete system.

questions: What would it mean for work to develop a person’s capacities rather than consume all the time and energy needed for them?
How might participation in benefits and decisions change the relationship between workers and owners?
When does an apparently private economic dispute become a matter of public concern?
How can the detailed examples be studied seriously while respecting the passages that leave arrangements open to future judgment?
What different contributions can fair institutions, voluntary generosity, and personal conduct make to shared prosperity?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the relationship between limits on concentrated wealth and protection of the poor.
Explore the demand to extend to others the protection one seeks for oneself.

references.label: 1 · Deuteronomy 24:14–15 — the worker’s need and timely wages
references.note: The passage makes the poor worker’s immediate dependence on wages a reason for prompt payment and includes the stranger within its concern. Compare this concrete obligation with the compilation’s broader discussion of shared benefits and public responsibility. How does attending to a worker’s lived circumstances change the meaning of an economic arrangement?

subjects.introduction: Socialism, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá once said, carries one fragrance from the leaves of the blessed tree, but the tree itself bears every fruit. The remark sets the terms for thinking about economic systems: what a programme gets right is not the whole of what religion intends. He foresaw that what socialists hoped to force would in time be done freely through faith and cooperation, warned that seizing the property of the rich would leave everyone hungry within a year, and watched democrats become extreme socialists and then Bolsheviks who took lives and public property alike. Preferring others to oneself is harder than enforced equality, because it depends on the willingness of the giver, and that is precisely why it lasts. A further caution warns against identifying a future Bahá’í commonwealth with any known system, left or right, and a later message asks the preachers of materialism, east and west, capitalist or socialist, where their promised new world is. Aristotle, long before, distinguished private possession from the generous common use of it, within a social order very unlike a vision of universal dignity [1]. The path continues toward the economic problem and its solution, voluntary giving, and the relations between labour and management.
subjects.arc: Begin with the limits of a political label, examine motives and means of reform, and end by placing generosity beside public protection.

order.why: Consider economic change through cooperation and willingness.
Open with the image of one fragrance within a larger tree.
Read the historical criticism of compulsory redistribution.
shortened: In America I said to the Socialists: 'These plans which you have will lead to no results. Suppose you take the property of the rich, what will you do after one year? All of you will be in need and will die from starvation. But it cannot be so for neither you nor the rich will be at rest.'

order.why: Discusses an international legislative settlement protecting both workers and capitalists, rather than resolving the issue through strikes alone.
Place political judgments within the revolutionary circumstances addressed.
shortened: In these days in Europe, especially in Russia, the Democratic Party has become extreme, and the Socialists have become radical, and the Bolsheviks have become oppressive. Now they have gone beyond freedom and have become bold in taking lives, seizing public property, and violating the chastity and virtue of pure and innocent women. It has become clear and evident that these people are Democrats in the beginning, extreme Socialists in the middle, and in the end become unfair Nihilists and Bolsheviks.

True Democrats are souls who seek the freedom of humanity, who hold to legitimate liberty, who establish constitutional government, and who desire good for all on earth. I hope they will take the path of moderation, abandon savagery, seek tranquility and pursue legitimate freedom.

order.why: Consider the instruction concerning party affiliation.
Explore the contrast between generosity and compulsion.
shortened: The principles of socialism are outstripped in the religions of God. For instance, God commands, 'But [they] prefer them [the poor] before themselves, although there be indigence among them' [Q59:9]. That is, the believers spend of their substance and share their possessions and prefer others to themselves willingly and with utmost spirituality. Socialists, however, desire to enforce equality and association by compulsion.

order.why: A reported comparison between redistribution by seizure and a system preserving ranks while affirming equal rights and the common good.
Proposes wages together with a share in profits as a practical arrangement between workers and capitalists.
Read the reported caution against identifying a future commonwealth with a known system.
Widen the critique to materialism across rival systems.
shortened: The time has come when those who preach the dogmas of materialism, whether of the east or the west, whether of capitalism or socialism, must give account of the moral stewardship they have presumed to exercise. Where is the "new world" promised by these ideologies? Where is the international peace to whose ideals they proclaim their devotion?

order.why: Consider another statement of that contrast.

questions: What ends should guide the evaluation of an economic system beyond its chosen label?
How do the passages bring voluntary generosity into conversation with the need for laws and institutions?
What care is needed when applying criticisms from particular historical debates to present circumstances?
How might a community investigate economic questions while remaining open about arrangements not yet determined?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the explicit distinction between economic principles and a complete technical system.
Consider social change as a work to which every group and individual can contribute.

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Politics II.5 — ownership, common use, and generosity
references.note: Aristotle distinguishes private possession from the generous sharing of its use and gives education and law a role in forming that disposition. Compare this with the compilation’s discussion of generosity and public arrangements. His ancient account also assumes social hierarchies, including slavery, that sharply distinguish its setting from a vision of universal human dignity.

subjects.displayTitle: Consent and the growth of a world order
subjects.introduction: A divine farmer sows seed and cannot gather the harvest the same afternoon; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá reaches for that image when asked how long Bahá’u’lláh’s vision of a renewed society will take, and reminds the impatient that the Cause of Christ needed three centuries. The pace is not the only constraint. The order Bahá’ís hope for is to come about by voluntary and democratic means or not at all: no imposing of principles through legislation, no violating of a country’s constitution, no forcing of a future minority to adopt the Faith, with the Universal House of Justice charged with safeguarding those limits. Bahá’u’lláh asks religious leaders and rulers to take counsel together over the needs of a sick world, and the Lesser Peace is expected to be built by nations still unaware of His name. Locke grounded political society in the consent of its members and then faced the harder problem of how such a society keeps acting together [1], a question this subject shares. What a person believes about humanity’s destiny is tested by how they treat those who do not share it. The journey continues into the growth of the Cause, into true liberty, and into the meaning of freedom.
subjects.arc: Begin with deliberation and gradual growth, place consent and minority rights at the center, and explore a future that must develop through participation.

order.why: Open with leaders deliberating together about the needs of humanity.
Consider the long timescale of religious development.
shortened: Grieve thou not over the slow advance of the Baha'i Cause in that land. This is but the early dawn. Consider how, with the Cause of Christ, three hundred years had to go by, before its great influence was made manifest. Today, not sixty years from its birth, the light of this Faith hath been shed around the planet.

order.why: Let the image of gradual growth frame the inquiry.
shortened: The Kingdom of peace, salvation, uprightness and reconciliation is founded in the Invisible World, and it will by degrees become manifest and apparent through the power of the Word of God!

order.why: Attend to possibilities still latent.
shortened: Now in this world of being, the Hand of Divine Power hath firmly laid the foundations of this all-highest Bounty and this wondrous Gift. Gradually whatsoever is latent in the innermost of this Holy Cycle shall appear and be made manifest, for now is but the beginning of its growth and the dayspring of the revelation of its Signs. Ere the close of this Century and of this Age, it shall be made clear and manifest how wondrous was that Springtide and how heavenly was that Gift!

order.why: Hear another account of gradual unfolding.
shortened: The point is, that the Cause of Baha'Ullah is inclusive of all perfections and supplies all the needs of the world of humanity. But this cannot be accomplished in a short time. Time is needed. This will gradually be realized.
When a divine farmer sows the seed, the crops cannot be immediately gathered in, but it is certain that the seed will develop into a harvest.

order.why: Connects legislation by the House of Justice with unanimous or majority decisions suited to changing circumstances.
Consider preparation through love before a fuller disclosure.
shortened: That which hath been recorded at God's behest in the Persian Bayan is indeed sufficient unto all, and none will be held to account for what it hath not commanded. Consider how numerous were those in the early days of the Revelation who obeyed, without the slightest deviation, every least one of its injunctions and yet reaped no benefit therefrom. The beginning of religion is love for God and for His Chosen Ones, and its end is to manifest that love to His servants.

order.why: Bring every person and group into the work of social change.
Read the explicit affirmation of voluntary and democratic development.
Consider change through constitutional processes.
Establish the obligation to respect governing authority and law.
Distinguish sharing principles from seeking their imposition.
Make minority rights and freedom from forced conversion central.
shortened: As to your question concerning the rights of the minority of non-Baha'i citizens in a Baha'i state, it is clear from the writings of our Faith that under a Baha'i system the rights of the minorities of any type must always be respected and upheld. Just as Baha'is today show obedience and loyalty to the government but refuse to bow to the majority if they are asked to deny their Faith, so in the future, when the majority is represented by the Faith the Baha'is will not force the minority to become followers of Baha'u'llah but they will expect the minority to be similarly obedient and loyal.

order.why: Read the discussion of a future majority in that context.
Consider the relation between nonpartisanship and a future social order.
Distinguish stages in the growth of world authority.
shortened: As you are no doubt aware, the Guardian indicated that the development of mankind from its present chaotic condition to the stage of Baha'i World Commonwealth would be a long and gradual one. The coming into existence of a World Authority and the initiation of the Lesser peace, is one major transformation in this process, and will be followed by other stages of the development of the Faith as outlined by Shoghi Effendi in his writings.

order.why: Explore peace emerging before a later religious world order.
shortened: Suffice it to say that this consummation will, by its very nature, be a gradual process, and must, as Baha'u'llah has Himself anticipated, lead at first to the establishment of that Lesser Peace which the nations of the earth, as yet unconscious of His Revelation and yet unwittingly enforcing the general principles which He has enunciated, will themselves establish.

order.why: Acknowledge the limits of premature specification.
Widen the timescale beyond the grasp of one generation.
Connect the larger prospect with gradual institutional development.
Consider the capacity of institutions to adapt.
Recognize the slow formation of a world civilization.
Explore development through the imagery of incubation and ferment.
Return to growth through a springtime landscape.
Give thoughtful scholarship a place in presenting new possibilities.
Close with practical social and economic development.

questions: What would make participation voluntary in practice, especially for people who do not share the majority’s beliefs?
How do minority rights test the sincerity of a commitment to a common social order?
What can a clear moral purpose offer when the eventual institutional arrangements remain uncertain?
How might gradual development call for both patience and action in the present?
What would it look like to invite every person and group into a shared effort without requiring agreement on its ultimate meaning?

neighbors.invitation: Distinguish an international executive from institutions associated with a later stage of development.
Consider the test of extending to others the protection one claims for oneself.

references.label: 1 · Locke, Second Treatise VIII, sections 95–99 — consent and political community
references.note: Locke grounds the formation of a political community in consent and then asks how that community can act together through majority decision. Compare this account with the compilation’s emphasis on voluntary development and protection of minorities. What questions remain when initial consent must become an ongoing life under shared institutions?

subjects.displayTitle: From decision to action: executive power
subjects.introduction: Knowing how a hotel should be built does not build it. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá names three things every undertaking needs: knowledge, decision, and the power to execute, and it is the third that most often fails. He then says something unexpected: the executive power that moves spirits, minds and souls today is love, the love of Bahá’u’lláh, which carries a law from the page into the heart. Shoghi Effendi carries the same question onto the scale of the planet. A world commonwealth will need a legislature, a tribunal and an executive able to carry decisions into effect, while the autonomy of nations and the freedom of individuals are completely safeguarded; and he is careful that the international executive of an earlier stage not be confused with Bahá’í institutions of a later one. Locke’s distinction between the occasional making of laws and their continuous execution offers a philosophical companion [1]. The question of how authority acts without devouring liberty leads on to the future of monarchy and the status of kings, and to the unity of governments on which any political unity depends.
subjects.arc: Begin with the gap between an idea and its realization, consider love as a moving power, and examine the institutional means of common action.

order.why: Open with a familiar project that requires more than knowledge.
shortened: "In the world of existence every undertaking is dependent upon the realization of three things. First, knowledge. Second, decision. Third, executive power. For example in building this hotel, first the plan was drawn. Second the company approved and decided upon the plan. Third, the capitalists put their money together to build it.

order.why: Complete humorous illustration of plans without the means to execute them.
Connects knowledge, will and action with the power needed for unity.
Introduce love as an inward power to accomplish change.
shortened: I beg of God that these philanthropic aims of yours may play a great effect in this world. Each program of laws is the result of legislation, but in order to carry it out there must needs be the Executive Power. To-day the penetrative or Executive Power over the spirits, minds and souls is the love of Baha’u’llah, because He is the Promised One of all the nations, the Heavenly Teacher of all the world and the Physician of the hearts and the souls.

order.why: Concise distinction between teaching and its executive power.
Explains prudent and practicable implementation of religious laws.
Directly distinguishes religious exposition from political execution.
Authoritative distinction between legislation and government enforcement.
Connects responsibility in government with spiritual accountability.
Complete medical-watchman story applies personal comfort versus duty to government.
Complete historical incident illustrates equal enforcement without privileged exceptions.
Explains why peace proposals need power of implementation.
Collective enforcement of peace and restraints on armaments.
Concrete composition and enforcement mechanism for an international tribunal.
Consider institutions capable of carrying common decisions into effect.
Distinguish the stages and institutions that should not be conflated.
Close with the fuller vision of authority serving a world community.
shortened: The unity of the human race, as envisaged by Baha'u'llah, implies the establishment of a world commonwealth in which all nations, races, creeds and classes are closely and permanently united, and in which the autonomy of its state members and the personal freedom and initiative of the individuals that compose them are definitely and completely safeguarded. This commonwealth must, as far as we can visualize it, consist of a world legislature, whose members will, as the trustees of the whole of mankind, ultimately control the entire resources of all the component nations, and will enact such laws as shall be required to regulate the life, satisfy the needs and adjust the relationships of all races and peoples. A world executive, backed by an international Force, will carry out the decisions arrived at, and apply the laws enacted by, this world legislature, and will safeguard the organic unity of the whole commonwealth.

questions: What usually stands between a sound decision and its realization, and how do the passages enlarge the answer?
How might love and institutional authority contribute differently to effective common action?
What safeguards and habits would help an executive body protect freedom while carrying out responsibilities that affect everyone?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the voluntary and democratic development of shared authority.
Explore a concrete case in which private relationships carry a public responsibility.

references.label: 1 · Locke, Second Treatise XII, sections 143–148 — execution of laws
references.note: Locke distinguishes the relatively intermittent making of laws from their continuing execution and also considers the conduct of external affairs. Compare the purposes of those distinctions with the compilation’s world institutions. How does the scale of a political community change the practical meaning of carrying out a common decision?

subjects.introduction: See with your own eyes and hear with your own ears: Bahá’u’lláh prays that His servants may be adorned with justice, and He means something this intimate. Fairness, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds, is the first quality of human nature, the one on which all other matters depend. Its enemies are not only tyrants but the quieter forces of desire, prejudice and inherited opinion, which bend what we perceive before we have said a word. The Qur’án sharpens the test by demanding equitable witness even toward a people one resents [1]. So fairmindedness turns out to be a discipline rather than a pleasant temperament: investigate for yourself, weigh evidence, speak without regard to inclination, and grant to others the protection you claim for yourself. The inward eye that learns to see justly soon finds itself answerable for conduct, for trusteeship over the earth’s people, for the honesty and trustworthiness of ordinary dealings, and for justice as it reaches into institutions and public life. Where the longing outruns the ability, there is a prayer for exactly this.
subjects.arc: Begin with independent seeing, confront the distortions of desire, and carry fairness outward into relationships, responsibility, and the search for truth.

order.why: Return to the fuller invitation to independent seeing.
Open with the invitation to see and hear for oneself.
Name fairness as a foundational human quality.
Preserve its separately supplied affirmation.
shortened: Likewise, from the Dawning-place of the utterance of the All-Merciful, say to the loved ones of God that the first quality of humanity is fairness, and all matters depend upon it.

order.why: Expose the blinding effect of prejudice and desire.
shortened: Beware lest desire deprive you of equity or prejudice cause you to rise up against God, the Protector, the Mighty, the Powerful.

order.why: Contrast fair speech with speech driven by inclination.
Bring the examination of evidence into view.
Use the image of opened eyes to deepen receptivity.
shortened: We beseech God to bestow the pure wine of fairness, that perchance it may open an eye and enable it to recognize Him.

order.why: Connect fair judgment with recognition of a new day.
shortened: We beseech God to adorn them with the ornament of justice and fairness that they may recognize this Day and what hath appeared therein.

order.why: Join calm self-reliance with brotherly counsel.
Turn scrutiny toward one’s own conduct.
shortened: Deal with one another with the utmost justice and equity. Transform treachery into trustworthiness, backbiting into self-purification, tyranny into justice, and heedlessness into remembrance.

order.why: Urges personal scrutiny, equity, honest testimony and freedom from idle imaginings.
Hear the brief call to kind and just treatment.
shortened: O Afnan! Regarding the blessed leaf who is related to you, you must treat her according to divine decree with kindness and justice - either summon them to Tehran or hasten yourself to Yazd.

order.why: Consider fairness in what is shared.
shortened: Share thou this among thy brothers, and in this sharing be praiseworthy and just, and be not an rejected oppressor.

order.why: Extend just conduct to everyone.
shortened: I hope you will always avoid tyranny and oppression, and that you will always uphold and practice justice towards all men and keep your hearts pure.

order.why: Connect fairness with service to fellow citizens.
shortened: To attain to true glory and honour, man should exercise justice and equity, forbear to act in an oppressive manner, render service to his government, and work for the good of his fellow-citizens.

order.why: Widen personal conduct into trusteeship for the earth’s people.
Relate justice to the fruits of human life and social order.
Keep justice present in every station.
shortened: Justice hath ever been and shall ever be beloved in every station.

order.why: Reject the way of tyranny.
Consider the consequences of oppression.
shortened: It is hoped that in gratitude for this divine confirmation, the foundation of justice will be established and the edifice of oppression will fall, the hands of the oppressors will be shortened and signs of justice and fairness will become manifest and clear, so that divine confirmation may continue and success may be sustained.

order.why: Apply justice to public authority.
Bring equity together with lovingkindness.
shortened: Be ye dawning-places of justice and equity and daysprings of loving-kindness and bounty unto all who are on earth.

order.why: Connect fairness with steadfast action.
Set passion beside the discipline of justice.
Imagine equity as a garment worn in daily life.
shortened: Then adorn thy body with the raiment of equity, which is among the garments of the All-Merciful between His near servants.

order.why: Consider justice as a gate to further understanding.
Give the aspiration the form of a prayer.
shortened: Beseech ye God that He may adorn all with the ornament of fairness and guide them with the light of justice.

order.why: Hear justice within the language of revelation.
shortened: The breezes of revelation have perfumed the world of justice and fairness, and the hand of power hath unlocked the doors of grace and bounty with the Most Great Name.

order.why: Close with a searching eye directed toward oneness.
Apply the protection one claims for oneself to women.

questions: How does the responsibility to investigate for oneself relate to the willingness to learn from others?
What desires or loyalties most easily distort a judgment, and how might we become aware of them?
Where do these passages move from fairness in perception to fairness in conduct and institutions?
How could the principle of extending to others the protection we seek for ourselves change a difficult relationship?

neighbors.invitation: Explore a reliance on inward perception that openly acknowledges the possibility of error.
Apply fair treatment to the rights of people who do not share a majority belief.

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 5:8 — justice despite hostility
references.note: The verse requires equitable witness even when hostility toward another people might tempt a person to depart from justice. Compare that demanding condition with the compilation’s warnings about desire and prejudice. What practices could make fairness reliable precisely when sympathy is absent or loyalties feel threatened?
